Cognitive Psychology · Theme 4 · Problem 4: Concepts

Semantic memory & concepts

Categories, typicality, prototypes and exemplars, semantic networks and spreading activation, and what semantic dementia reveals: every concept, study and example

Dear Sezen,

Theme 4 is about how your mind stores meaning. Three readings attack the same question from three sides. Murphy (NOBA, Categories and Concepts) looks at single categories: why they can’t be defined, why a robin is a ‘better’ bird than a penguin, why we say ‘chair’ rather than ‘furniture’, and whether we store averages, examples or theories. Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207) zooms out to the whole network of knowledge: nodes, links and spreading activation, then the classical, prototype, exemplar and essentialist approaches again, with their problems. Bozeat et al. (2003) watch the network fall apart in semantic dementia, using drawings like a duck with four legs.

This matters beyond the exam: every recommendation feed you scroll, every stereotype you resist and every quick ‘that’s a…’ judgement runs on the machinery in this theme.

How to read this platform. The Lessons panel has three tabs: 📖 Full lectures (34 screens, reading by reading, every concept and study), 🎯 Learning objectives (A1–A4, B1–B3, C1–C2, each answered with a model answer) and 🧠 In-depth questions (the Scattergories warm-up, Bron A 1–6, Bron B 1–4, Bron C 1–5 and the true/false exit, each with the Dutch question, an English translation, triage and a hidden model answer). On every screen look at the diagram first, read the bullets, say the hook out loud, then open the chips. Values marked illustrative only show a shape; all other numbers come from your readings.

— Your professor

🗺️ The big picture in one paragraph: Picture your knowledge as a city map 🗺️. Each place is a concept (‘bird’, ‘chair’, ‘duck’), places that are alike are built close together, and roads connect things that go together. Murphy zooms in on one neighbourhood: how is BIRD laid out, with robins in the centre and penguins at the edge? Robinson-Riegler studies the roads: how activity travels from ‘yellow’ to ‘lemon’ and why ‘a robin is a bird’ is answered faster. Bozeat et al. watch a disease slowly erase the map: the side streets (what makes a duck a duck) vanish first, while the main avenues (what all animals share) survive longest.

📚 Key Terms: read these first

TermPlain-language definition
Semantic memoryGeneral knowledge of objects, facts, concepts and word meanings, not tied to when you learned it
CategoryA set of entities treated as equivalent in some way; members are usually similar
ConceptThe mental representation of a category
Classical viewA concept is a definition: necessary and jointly sufficient features; all-or-none membership
Fuzzy boundaryUnclear, shifting category edges with borderline members (Hampton, 1979)
TypicalityGraded ‘goodness’ of members, from the prototype (robin) to borderline members (penguin)
Family resemblanceTypical items share many features with the category and few with other categories (Rosch & Mervis, 1975)
Basic levelThe preferred, intermediate level of categorisation (chair), the most differentiated
Prototype theoryA summary representation of features weighted by frequency (Smith & Medin, 1981)
Exemplar theoryA concept is the set of stored examples; classify by summed similarity (Medin & Schaffer, 1978)
Knowledge approachConcepts fit world knowledge; coherent concepts are learned faster (Murphy & Allopenna, 1994)
Psychological essentialismBelief that members have a hidden essence that causes their features (Keil, 1989)
Semantic networkConcept nodes joined by links that represent relationships
Spreading activationActivation of one node spreads to linked nodes, decaying with time, distance and number of nodes (Collins & Loftus, 1975)
Category / feature verificationSpeeded true/false judgements (‘A robin is a bird’, ‘A cat has skin’); RT reveals closeness
Semantic primingProcessing one stimulus speeds processing of a related one (yellow → lemon)
Natural kind · artifact · ad hoc · metaphoricalCategory types ordered by member similarity (Goldstone & Kersten, 2003)
Semantic dementiaProgressive, selective loss of conceptual knowledge with anterior temporal atrophy
Shared vs distinctive featureFeature true of many concepts (wings, eyes) vs of one or a few (a mallard’s green feathers)
Omission / intrusionA target feature left out of a drawing / a wrong feature added (four legs on a duck)
Letter fluency (FAS)Say as many words starting with F, A, S in 1 min each: a test of executive function

🧵 Synthesis

One thesis for the whole theme: semantic knowledge is a web of overlapping features and links in which similarity does most of the work. Murphy shows the shape of single categories: no definitions, fuzzy edges, graded typicality explained by family resemblance, a preferred basic level, and a pull from world knowledge and essentialist beliefs. Robinson-Riegler shows the wiring: concept nodes joined by links of different strengths, with activation that spreads, fades, sums and fires at a threshold, which gives you typicality effects in verification and semantic priming. Bozeat et al. show the building material: when semantic dementia erodes the network, distinctive features go first and features shared across many concepts survive and even intrude (a duck with four legs), exactly as a distributed, feature-based, prototype-like system predicts.

How the pieces connect: typicality = feature overlap (Rosch & Mervis) = short network links (Collins & Loftus) = the robust core that survives in SD (Bozeat). Prototype vs exemplar is a trade-off between economy and detail, which is why the field now favours multiple systems. Similarity is powerful but not everything: essences (Keil, Rips) and knowledge (donker vs blegdav) can override it.

Readings: Murphy, G. (2021). Categories and concepts. NOBA · Robinson-Riegler & Robinson-Riegler, Networks and Concepts: The Classification Database (pp. 198–207) · Bozeat, S., et al. (2003). A duck with four legs. Cognitive Neuropsychology, 20(1), 27–47.

Lecture 1 of 34 · objectives A1

🗂️ Categories and concepts: the building blocks

What they are and why intelligent behaviour depends on them

❓ This lecture answers: What are categories and concepts, and why could we not think or act intelligently without them?
↳ How it fits: This sets up the whole theme: a concept is your mental file for a category, and it lets you use what you know about a few things to handle endless new ones.
  • A category is a set of objects that can be treated as equivalent in some way; useful categories share many properties (trucks, trout, weddings).
  • A concept is the mental representation of a category. Usually concept ≈ category, but someone’s concept can be wrong.
  • Concepts let you extend what you learned about a few objects to a potentially infinite set of new ones (the new classroom, the halogen bulb).
  • We learn thousands of categories without study, yet programming a computer to do this is hard, because category members are surprisingly diverse.
  • Animals and infants also have concepts (Mareschal, Quinn & Lea, 2010), e.g. a squirrel’s concept of predators, but far fewer, and none like ‘mortgage’.
🪝 Memory hook: Category = the club 🌍; concept = your membership list in your head 🧠.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Concepts are the core of intelligent behaviour: they let us treat new things as instances of what we already know.
Tap to open ▸
A category is a group of things out in the world, like all trucks. A concept is the idea of that group in your head. Because you have the idea, you know what to do with a truck you’ve never seen.
TermMeaningExample
Categoryset of entities treated as equivalent; usually similartrucks, psychopaths, trout
Conceptmental representation of a categorymy idea of ‘truck’
Generalisationextending a fact about some members to othershalogen bulb → all projectors
Who has concepts?humans, infants, animals (fewer, simpler)squirrel’s ‘predator’ concept

🧩 Comprehension check

What is the difference between a category and a concept?

A category is the set of things in the world; a concept is the mental representation of that set.

Why do concepts matter for behaviour?

They let us know what new objects are and how to act toward them, and to generalise facts to unseen members.

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 2 of 34 · objectives A2 · A3

📏 The classical view: categories as definitions

Necessary and jointly sufficient features

❓ This lecture answers: Can a category be captured by a strict definition, a checklist every member must pass?
↳ How it fits: Here the theme gets its first test: the oldest answer says concepts are definitions, but for most everyday categories no such checklist can be found.
  • Traditional assumption: categories are well-defined by a definition with two parts.
  • Necessary features: what every member must have. Jointly sufficient: anything with all of them is a member.
  • For most familiar categories no definition can be found: not all dogs have four legs or bark; necessary features (blood, breathing) are not sufficient.
  • Even science and law struggle: Pluto (2006) showed there is no hard-and-fast definition of a planet.
  • Membership in this view is all-or-none: you are in or out, with no ‘better’ members.
🪝 Memory hook: Classical view = a bouncer with a checklist ✅: tick every box or you’re out.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Definitions work for formal concepts, but most natural categories cannot be defined by necessary and sufficient features.
Tap to open ▸
The old idea was that every category has a dictionary definition, like ‘a dog is a four-legged animal that barks’. But then a three-legged, silent dog wouldn’t be a dog, which is silly.
Claim of the classical viewProblem (Murphy)
Every member has the necessary featuresthree-legged dogs, dogs that don’t bark
Having all features guarantees membershipblood + breathing also fits you
Experts can define their categoriesPluto: no agreed definition of planet
Membership is all-or-noneborderline items and typicality (next lectures)
▶ Categories and concepts Rosch cognitive psychology▶ Murphy categories and concepts NOBA▶ classical view of concepts necessary sufficient features(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What do ‘necessary’ and ‘jointly sufficient’ mean?

Necessary: every member must have the feature. Jointly sufficient: anything that has all the features is a member.

What does the Pluto debate illustrate?

That even scientists could not give a clear definition of a familiar category (planet).

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 3 of 34 · objectives A1 · A3

🌫️ Fuzzy boundaries and borderline items

Hampton (1979) and McCloskey & Glucksberg (1978)

❓ This lecture answers: Do categories have sharp edges, or are some items only barely in or barely out?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L2: if people disagree about sinks and olives, and even change their own minds, then categories are fuzzy and a strict definition cannot be how concepts work.
  • Hampton (1979): items were not clear members or non-members; many were barely in or barely out, with much disagreement.
  • Sinks barely counted as kitchen utensils; sponges were barely excluded. Seaweed just counted as a vegetable; tomatoes and gourds just did not.
  • Members and non-members formed a continuum, with no obvious break; if categories were well defined, such items should be rare.
  • McCloskey & Glucksberg (1978): the same judgement two weeks later (‘Is an olive a fruit?’) changed for borderline items up to 22% of the time.
  • Conclusion: categories are fuzzy, with unclear boundaries that can shift over time.
🪝 Memory hook: Category edges are a fog bank 🌫️, not a fence.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Borderline items, and people’s inconsistency about them, show that category boundaries are fuzzy rather than defined.
Tap to open ▸
Ask people if a sink is a kitchen utensil and they hesitate; ask again in two weeks and some change their answer. If categories had real definitions, that wouldn’t happen.
📄 Hampton (1979)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why are borderline items a problem for the classical view?

A definition sorts every item cleanly in or out, so there should be no items that are barely in or barely out.

What does a 22% change rate show?

That boundaries are unstable within the same person, so categories are fuzzy.

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 4 of 34 · objectives A1 · A4

🎯 Typicality: graded membership

Some members are ‘better’ examples (Rosch, 1973)

❓ This lecture answers: Why do some members, like a robin, feel like better examples of a category than others, like a penguin?
↳ How it fits: This shows that membership is graded, not all-or-none, and typicality turns out to predict how fast we categorise, learn and name things.
  • Even among clear members, some seem better than others (Rosch, 1973): robins and sparrows are very typical birds; ostriches and penguins are atypical.
  • Typicality is found simply by asking people (Table 1 of Murphy: furniture and fruit ordered by Rosch & Mervis, 1975); people agree strongly.
  • It is perhaps the most important variable: it predicts categorisation speed, learning order, membership judgements, naming order and understanding.
  • The most typical member is the category prototype; items less similar to it become less typical.
  • Typicality and borderline members are two sides of the same coin: very atypical items (a rug as furniture) become so atypical that membership is doubted.
🪝 Memory hook: From robin 🐦 to penguin 🐧: a sliding scale, not a yes/no.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Category membership is graded: typicality is the central variable, and its far end produces the borderline items.
Tap to open ▸
Everyone agrees a penguin is a bird, but it feels like a ‘worse’ bird than a robin. That feeling of ‘how good an example is it?’ is typicality, and it affects how fast you think about things.

🧩 Comprehension check

Why are typicality and borderline membership ‘two sides of the same coin’?

As items become less similar to the prototype they become less typical, and at the extreme so atypical that membership becomes uncertain.

Name three things typicality influences.

Speed of categorisation, order of learning, how often items are judged members (also naming order and comprehension).

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 5 of 34 · objectives A4

👪 Where typicality comes from: family resemblance

Rosch & Mervis (1975) and the frequency question

❓ This lecture answers: What makes a member typical: simply seeing it often, or sharing many features with its category and few with others?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L4: typicality comes mainly from family resemblance, the overlap of features, which hints that concepts are organised around shared features.
  • Is typicality just frequency (we see more robins)? Frequency has some effect but is not the most important variable (Rosch, Simpson & Miller, 1976): rugs and tables are seen equally often.
  • Family resemblance theory (Rosch & Mervis, 1975): an item is typical if it (a) has features frequent in its category and (b) lacks features frequent in other categories.
  • Robins share the shape, size, parts and behaviour common among birds; penguins lack them and share features with fish (swimming, fin-like wings).
  • Experiment 1: artificial-category items with common features were learned first and rated more typical.
  • Experiment 2: the more features an item shared with another category, the longer it took to learn. Both parts of the theory are supported.
🪝 Memory hook: Typical = looks like the family 👪 and not like the neighbours 🏠.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Typicality reflects feature overlap with the category and lack of overlap with other categories, not mere frequency.
Tap to open ▸
A robin is a typical bird not because you see lots of robins, but because it has what most birds have and nothing that belongs to other animals. A penguin swims like a fish, so it feels less bird-like.
📄 Rosch & Mervis (1975)

🧩 Comprehension check

What are the two parts of family resemblance theory?

Typical items (a) have features frequent in the category and (b) do not have features frequent in other categories.

Why is the penguin atypical according to Rosch and Mervis?

It lacks common bird features and has features common in fish (swimming, fin-like wings).

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 6 of 34 · objectives A1

🪜 Category hierarchies and the basic level

Rosch et al. (1976): the preferred, ‘just right’ level

❓ This lecture answers: A chair is also furniture and a desk chair, so which level do we naturally use to name and think about things?
↳ How it fits: This adds structure to the theme: concepts sit in hierarchies, and one ‘just right’ basic level is named first, learned first and recognised fastest.
  • Many categories form hierarchies: brown bear ⊂ bear ⊂ mammal ⊂ vertebrate ⊂ animal ⊂ entity; artifacts too (desk chair ⊂ chair ⊂ furniture ⊂ artifact ⊂ object).
  • Any object belongs to many categories at once, but there is usually one preferred label: ‘Move that chair’ (Brown, 1958).
  • This is the basic level (Rosch, Mervis, Gray, Johnson & Boyes-Braem, 1976): a ‘Goldilocks’ level, not too small, not too big.
  • Naming pictures: 1,595 basic names, 14 subordinate, 1 superordinate. Basic labels are also most frequent in text (Wisniewski & Murphy, 1989).
  • Basic categories are learned first by children (Anglin, 1977; superordinates are especially hard) and identified fastest.
🪝 Memory hook: Basic level = Goldilocks’ porridge 🥣: chair, not furniture or desk chair.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Categories are nested in hierarchies, and the intermediate basic level is privileged for naming, learning and identification.
Tap to open ▸
Your desk chair is also ‘furniture’ and an ‘object’, but you’d say ‘chair’. That middle level is the one we name, learn and recognise most easily.
LevelExampleStatus
Superordinatefurniture · animalfew shared features; hard for children
Basicchair · bear · birdnamed first, learned first, identified fastest
Subordinatedesk chair · brown bearvery similar to sibling categories

What is the basic level of ‘northern brown bear’?

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 7 of 34 · objectives A1

🧭 Why the basic level? Differentiation, culture and expertise

The basic level is in the eye of the beholder

❓ This lecture answers: Why is one level ‘basic’, and why does that level shift with culture and expertise?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L6: the basic level is the most useful split, members alike but different from neighbours, so how our knowledge is organised depends partly on what we know.
  • Rosch first proposed that the basic level ‘cuts the world at its joints’, reflecting big real differences (chairs vs tables, cats vs mice).
  • But it is not universal: less industrialised societies use specific names like elm, trout, finch (Berlin, 1992); industrialised people know less nature, so the basic level ‘moved up’.
  • Experts prefer a more specific level: birdwatchers say sparrow, carpenters say roofing hammer (Tanaka & Taylor, 1991).
  • Explanation: basic categories are most differentiated: members are similar to each other but different from other categories (Murphy & Brownell, 1985).
  • Superordinates have too little in common; subordinates are too similar to their neighbours. Footnote: whether infants learn superordinates first is debated (Mandler, 2004).
🪝 Memory hook: Basic level = the best trade-off ⚖️: alike inside, different outside.
★ KEY INSIGHT · The basic level is the most differentiated level, and since differentiation depends on knowledge, it shifts with culture and expertise.
Tap to open ▸
‘Chair’ wins because all chairs look alike and don’t look like tables. ‘Furniture’ is too mixed; ‘desk chair’ is too close to ‘dining chair’. But a carpenter, who knows more, finds the specific level just as easy.

Subordinate (desk chair)very highlow (desk vs dining chair)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why are superordinate categories less useful?

Their members are not very similar to one another: few features are common to most furniture.

What does expertise show about the basic level?

That it depends on knowledge, not only on the world: experts find more specific categories most differentiated.

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 8 of 34 · objectives A2 · A3 · A4

⭐ Prototype theory: a summary representation

Weighted features and matching (Smith & Medin, 1981)

❓ This lecture answers: Could a concept be one summary description of the whole category, a list of weighted features?
↳ How it fits: This is the first full answer to what is inside a concept: a prototype explains typicality and fuzzy borders by how well an item matches the summary.
  • Prototype theory: people store a summary representation, a description meant to apply to the category as a whole.
  • It is a set of weighted features (Smith & Medin, 1981): wings and feathers weigh a lot, eating worms less, living in Antarctica little but not zero.
  • We can state such generalisations and learn them from statements (‘the Komodo dragon can grow to 10 feet’).
  • To classify, you (unconsciously) check how well an item matches each concept’s weighted list.
  • Typical items have more, higher-weighted features → easier match; borderline items match several categories or none well (edible seaweed).
🪝 Memory hook: Prototype = a police composite sketch 🖼️ of the whole category.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A prototype is an abstract summary of weighted features; graded matching to it explains typicality and fuzzy boundaries.
Tap to open ▸
Your brain keeps one ‘average bird’ description with the most important bird features. Anything that fits it well, like a robin, gets recognised as a bird quickly.
PhenomenonPrototype explanation
Typicalitytypical items share more, higher-weighted features with the summary
Uncertainty about atypical itemsfewer or lower-weighted features, and features of other concepts
Borderline itemsmatch several categories, or none well (seaweed)
Learning from statementsgeneral descriptions add directly to the summary
▶ Categories and concepts Rosch cognitive psychology▶ Murphy categories and concepts NOBA▶ prototype theory concepts(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What does ‘weighted’ mean in prototype theory?

Each feature is weighted by its frequency in the category, so common features count more in the match.

Why is ‘summary’ the important word?

The theory claims one description for the whole category, unlike exemplar theory, which stores no summary.

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 9 of 34 · objectives A2 · A3 · A4

🗃️ Exemplar theory and the verdict: multiple systems

Medin & Schaffer (1978); Allen & Brooks (1991)

❓ This lecture answers: Or is a concept simply all the examples we remember, and which view do the studies support?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L8: exemplars win many lab tests, but the verdict is that we probably use several systems, summaries and stored examples, depending on the situation.
  • Exemplar theory (Medin & Schaffer, 1978) denies a summary: your concept of vegetables is the remembered vegetables you have seen (perhaps hundreds or thousands).
  • Classification: compare the object with exemplars in memory, add up similarity scores per category, choose the highest.
  • Why propose it? Lab learners see the same exemplars again and again and probably memorise them (Smith & Minda, 1998); Allen & Brooks (1991): similarity to an old item overrode a taught rule.
  • Exemplar theory wins most lab comparisons, but labs use few exemplars seen repeatedly; real life has little study of each squirrel or chair, and we also learn from general statements.
  • Current view: multiple systems: summary descriptions (‘dogs have four legs’), exemplars (your family dog, Lassie) and rules (a strike in baseball).
🪝 Memory hook: Prototype = one composite sketch 🖼️; exemplar = the whole photo album 📸.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Exemplar theory stores examples, not summaries; the evidence suggests concepts combine exemplars, summaries and rules.
Tap to open ▸
Instead of one ‘average vegetable’, maybe you remember lots of vegetables you’ve seen. A new thing on your plate counts as a vegetable if it looks like many of them.
📄 Allen & Brooks (1991)

🧩 Comprehension check

How does exemplar theory classify an object?

It computes the object’s similarity to each stored exemplar, sums these per category, and picks the category with the highest total.

Why do many researchers favour multiple systems?

Some knowledge comes from general statements (summary), some from memorable exemplars, and some categories involve rules.

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 10 of 34 · objectives A1 · A3

🧩 The knowledge approach: donkers and blegdavs

Concepts must fit what we know about the world

❓ This lecture answers: Do features have to make sense together with what we already know for a concept to be learned easily?
↳ How it fits: This shows that concepts are not just lists of features: they are tied to our world knowledge, which speeds learning but can also mislead us.
  • Prototype and exemplar theories treat features as arbitrary: people ‘just learn them’, whatever they are.
  • Murphy & Allopenna (1994): concepts whose features make sense together (donker, an underwater building) are learned much faster than incoherent ones (blegdav, a desert building reached by submarine).
  • Features that seem connected (underwater + submarine) are learned better than unrelated ones (being red).
  • So we try to connect new concepts to existing world knowledge; an animal that doesn’t eat or reproduce would puzzle you.
  • Knowledge helps (learning tablets from laptops and phones) but can mislead (expecting a tablet to do what your phone did).
🪝 Memory hook: Donker = a story that makes sense 📖; blegdav = a random word list 🎲.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Concepts are embedded in our world knowledge, which speeds learning of coherent concepts: something prototype and exemplar theories don’t predict.

If someone describes a building that’s underwater and reached by submarine, you get it instantly. A desert building reached by submarine with polar bears as pets is hard to learn because nothing fits.

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is the blegdav hard to learn?

Its features don’t fit together with world knowledge (submarines in a desert, polar bears as pets), so they can’t be integrated.

What do prototype and exemplar theories fail to predict here?

That the content of features matters: they put no constraints on which descriptions or exemplars are learned.

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 11 of 34 · objectives A2 · A3

🧬 Psychological essentialism

Keil (1989): a raccoon can’t change its stripes

❓ This lecture answers: Why do we believe a raccoon stays a raccoon even when it is changed to look like a skunk?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L10: for natural kinds people assume a hidden essence decides membership, so what something looks like is not the whole story.
  • Psychological essentialism: people believe some categories (especially natural kinds: animals, plants, minerals) have an underlying property found only in that category that causes its other features.
  • Most categories don’t actually have essences, but the belief is firmly held; membership then depends on the assumed cause, not only visible features.
  • Keil (1989): a raccoon altered to look and smell like a skunk is still a raccoon (adults and children over 4); a coffeepot altered into a bird feeder is a bird feeder: artifacts have no essence.
  • Signs: (a) in or out, no in-between; (b) resistance to change of membership or essence-linked properties; (c) for living things, essence passes to offspring.
  • Helpful for nature, harmful for people: groups seen as having essences (‘bad blood’) → differences exaggerated, discrimination justified (Hirschfeld, 1996).
🪝 Memory hook: A raccoon in a skunk costume is still a raccoon 🦝: the essence is under the fur.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Essentialism shows that categorisation can depend on beliefs about hidden causes, not only on visible similarity, mostly for natural kinds.
Tap to open ▸
People believe there is a hidden ‘something’, like DNA, that makes a dog a dog. So if you surgically make a raccoon look like a skunk, everyone still says it’s a raccoon. For a coffeepot turned into a bird feeder, nobody cares about its ‘true nature’.
📄 Keil (1989)
ElementDetail
QuestionDo people believe in hidden essences?
MethodAdults and children heard about a raccoon transformed to look and smell like a skunk, and a coffeepot turned into a bird feeder
Findingsraccoon: still a raccoon (adults and children over 4); coffeepot: now a bird feeder
Conclusionnatural kinds are believed to have essences; artifacts are not
Why it mattersappearance alone does not decide membership

🧩 Comprehension check

Why does the raccoon stay a raccoon but the coffeepot doesn’t stay a coffeepot?

People believe natural kinds have an unchangeable hidden essence, while artifacts are defined by function and have no essence.

Name the three signs of essentialism.

Membership is all-or-none; membership and essence-linked properties resist change; for living things the essence passes to offspring.

Part A · Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)
Lecture 12 of 34 · objectives A1 · A2

🧵 Conclusion: concepts in everyday life

Multiple processes, brain systems and cultures

❓ This lecture answers: How do all these pieces, examples, summaries, knowledge and rules, come together in concepts we use every day?
↳ How it fits: This closes Part A: real concepts combine several kinds of information, probably handled by different brain systems, with some influence of culture.
  • Concepts are central to everyday thought: planning and remembering are done in terms of categories (visiting a friend’s new baby: what it will do, what gifts fit).
  • Concept learning combines exemplars (babies you’ve seen), general descriptions, world knowledge (babies have kidneys) and occasional rules (rooting reflex).
  • These aspects are probably handled by different neural structures (Maddox & Ashby, 2004).
  • Culture: different interests may shape concepts (East vs West thought; Norenzayan, Smith, Kim & Nisbett, 2002), but cultures share chairs, dogs, parties and jars.
  • Outside resources: Barsalou’s (1983) goal categories, e.g. ‘things to carry out of a burning house’: what is their prototype?
🪝 Memory hook: One concept, four feeders 🍼: examples, descriptions, knowledge, rules.
★ KEY INSIGHT · No single theory is complete: concepts arise from several cognitive and neural systems working together.
Tap to open ▸
You know what to expect from a baby you’ve never met because your ‘baby’ concept is built from babies you’ve seen, things you’ve read, general knowledge and a few rules.

🧩 Comprehension check

Which brain-level claim does Murphy make?

That the different aspects of concepts are probably accomplished by different neural structures (Maddox & Ashby, 2004).

Why might cultural differences in concepts be smaller than some experiments suggest?

Different cultures share many common categories (chairs, dogs, parties, jars) and the world’s structure constrains useful categories.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 13 of 34 · objectives B1

🕸️ Semantic networks and verification tasks

How knowledge is stored, and how we measure it

❓ This lecture answers: How might knowledge be stored as a network of linked ideas, and how can response speed reveal it?
↳ How it fits: Part B turns to how concepts are linked: a robin is verified as a bird faster than a penguin, suggesting closer links in the network.
  • A popular metaphor: knowledge is stored as associative networks of nodes (concepts or features) joined by links; related concepts are figuratively ‘close’.
  • Category verification: verify ‘A penguin is a bird’ or ‘A robin is a bird’ as fast as possible → how we access category knowledge.
  • Feature verification: ‘A cat has pointy ears’ vs ‘A cat has skin’ → how features are stored and accessed.
  • Speed, not accuracy, is the informative measure: the questions are easy and errors are rare unless people rush.
  • Robin is verified faster than penguin, pointy ears faster than skin: robin is more tightly connected to ‘bird’, ears are closer to ‘cat’.
🪝 Memory hook: A semantic network is a metro map 🚇: stations = concepts, lines = relations.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Verification reaction times reveal the structure of the network: closer concepts are verified faster.
Tap to open ▸
Imagine all your knowledge as dots joined by strings. Scientists can’t see the strings, but they can time how fast you say ‘true’ to ‘a robin is a bird’: the faster, the shorter the string.
TaskExampleWhat it revealsFinding
Category verification‘A robin is a bird’how category membership is accessedrobin faster than penguin
Feature verification‘A cat has pointy ears’how features are storedpointy ears faster than skin
Dependent variablereaction timeerrors are rarespeed = closeness

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is accuracy not the main measure in verification tasks?

The statements are easy, so people almost never err unless they answer too quickly; speed varies informatively.

What does faster verification of ‘A cat has pointy ears’ than ‘A cat has skin’ show?

That pointy ears are stored closer to (more strongly linked with) the concept cat than skin is.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 14 of 34 · objectives B1

🧠 Semantic networks vs neural networks

Kindred spirits, different levels

❓ This lecture answers: Is a semantic network a map of the brain, or a convenient picture of how meanings connect?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L13: semantic networks describe links between meanings, while neural networks describe brain-like wiring; both share the idea that activation travels along links.
  • ‘Close to’ in a semantic network is figurative: canary is close to bird in meaning, not in the brain.
  • Semantic network models are not based on brain structure, unlike neural network models.
  • Neural networks: nodes correspond to neurons; nodes and links are not dedicated to particular words (no ‘canary neuron’).
  • Semantic networks: nodes are specific concepts (canary) and links are relationships (canary → pet); retrieval = gliding along links.
  • Shared idea: excitatory connections; activation spreads (and in neural networks can also inhibit).
🪝 Memory hook: Semantic network = a mind map ✏️; neural network = the wiring under the floor 🔌.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Semantic networks are a convenient metaphor for relations among concepts; they share spreading activation with neural networks but are not brain models.
Tap to open ▸
A semantic network is a drawing of ideas and how they relate. A neural network is a model of brain cells. Both say ‘when one part lights up, connected parts light up too’, but only the semantic one has a dot labelled ‘canary’.
Semantic networkNeural network
A node isa specific concept (canary)a neuron-like unit
A link isa relationship (canary → pet)a connection weight between units
Dedicated to words?yesno
Based on brain structure?no (metaphor)yes
Retrievalspreading activation along linksactivation (or inhibition) of units

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is ‘close to’ in quotation marks in semantic networks?

It means related in meaning, not physically near in the brain.

What do the two network types have in common?

Both use excitatory connections so that activating one representation activates related ones.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 15 of 34 · objectives B1 · B3

⚡ The spreading activation model

Collins & Loftus (1975): four processing assumptions

❓ This lecture answers: How does retrieving one concept spread to related ones, according to Collins and Loftus?
↳ How it fits: This explains how the network is used: activation spreads, fades with distance and time, adds up, and switches on a concept once it passes a threshold.
  • Exemplified by Collins & Loftus (1975): concept nodes linked in an associative network.
  • Links represent many relations: membership (canary → bird), property (yellow → canary) and subtler ones (canary – cat).
  • Presenting a concept activates its node; activation spreads to linked concepts.
  • Activation decreases with time, distance and the number of concepts activated (the more concepts, the less each receives).
  • Activation reaching a node is summed; past a threshold that concept is activated.
🪝 Memory hook: Spreading activation = ripples in a pond 🌊: they spread, weaken and add up where they meet.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Retrieval is spreading activation that decays, sums and triggers concepts at a threshold.
Tap to open ▸
Think of dropping a stone in a pond. The ripple moves out to nearby ideas, gets weaker the further it goes, and when two ripples meet at the same idea they add up. If enough arrives, that idea pops into your mind.
AssumptionMeaningConsequence
Spreadactivation travels along linksrelated concepts become active
Decayweaker with time, distance and number of conceptsdistant concepts get little
Summationactivation from several paths adds upwell-connected concepts reach threshold sooner
Thresholda concept fires when its sum passes a valueexplains priming head starts
▶ semantic network spreading activation Collins Loftus▶ Robinson-Riegler concepts categories(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Name the three factors that weaken activation.

Time, distance in the network and the number of concepts activated.

Why does summation matter?

A concept reached by several paths collects more activation and passes threshold sooner.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 16 of 34 · objectives B3

🍋 Semantic priming

Processing one item speeds processing of a related one

❓ This lecture answers: Why do we recognise ‘lemon’ faster right after seeing ‘yellow’?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L15: priming is the visible result of spreading activation, giving strong everyday evidence that related concepts really are linked.
  • Semantic priming (introduced in Chapter 2): processing one stimulus enhances or speeds up processing of a related stimulus.
  • A prime (‘yellow’) activates its node; activation spreads to related concepts such as sun, canary, lemon.
  • This gives them a head start toward their threshold for identification.
  • When ‘lemon’ is then presented, the person is almost ready (‘primed and ready’) to verify it as a word.
  • Unrelated words (table) get no head start. The associative-network architecture is now part of many accounts of knowledge and cognition.
🪝 Memory hook: Priming = pre-heating the oven 🔥: the cake (lemon) bakes faster.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Priming follows from spreading activation: related concepts get a head start toward threshold.
Tap to open ▸
When you read ‘yellow’, your brain quietly warms up related ideas like lemon and sun. So if ‘lemon’ comes next, you recognise it a split second faster than ‘table’.
StepWhat happens in the network
1 · prime ‘yellow’YELLOW node activated
2 · spreadactivation reaches SUN, CANARY, LEMON (not TABLE)
3 · head startLEMON is partly charged, below threshold
4 · target ‘lemon’small extra input → threshold → fast response
Unrelated ‘table’starts from zero → slower

Why is ‘lemon’ recognised faster after ‘yellow’ than after ‘chair’?

Yellow is linked to lemon, so spreading activation pre-charges LEMON toward its threshold; chair isn’t linked.

Which processing assumption makes priming weaker for distant concepts?

Activation decays with distance (and time and number of concepts activated).

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 17 of 34 · objectives B1

🧱 The functions of concepts

Medin & Rips (2005): understanding, prediction, learning, communication

❓ This lecture answers: What jobs do concepts do for us: understanding, predicting, learning new things and communicating?
↳ How it fits: This shows why the organisation of knowledge matters: concepts are the building blocks that let us recognise, predict and talk about new things.
  • Robinson-Riegler moves from the whole network to specific concepts: what gives a category its structure (why are Monopoly, dodge ball and hopscotch all games)?
  • ‘Concepts are the building blocks of thought’ (Solomon, Medin & Lynch, 1999); Medin & Rips (2005) list their functions.
  • Understanding: mental shorthand. Prediction: ‘reality show’ lets you infer real people, competition, prize money, and that you won’t like it.
  • Learning: concepts support new learning (reality shows weren’t a category 20 years ago).
  • Communication: we combine concepts in language (‘restaurant coffee’ vs ‘real coffee’).
🪝 Memory hook: Concepts do 4 jobs: U-P-L-C ⚙️: Understand, Predict, Learn, Communicate.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Concepts go far beyond labels: they let us understand, infer, learn and communicate efficiently.
Tap to open ▸
If a friend says ‘it’s a reality show’, you instantly know a dozen things about it without being told. That’s concepts working as shortcuts, prediction machines and conversation tools.

Give an example of concepts supporting prediction.

Knowing a show is a ‘reality show’ lets you infer unstated features (real people, competition) and predict whether you’ll like it.

What question about Monopoly, dodge ball and hopscotch opens the section?

What makes them all games despite their different characteristics: what gives a category its structure?

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 18 of 34 · objectives B1 · B2

🧳 Categories as a concept: four types

Natural kinds, artifacts, ad hoc and metaphorical categories

❓ This lecture answers: Are all categories built the same way, or do natural kinds, artifacts, goal-based and metaphorical categories differ?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L17: categories differ in how similar their members are, from flowers to ‘things to take on vacation’, so no single rule fits them all.
  • Categories themselves form a concept: there are types of categories (Medin, Lynch & Solomon, 2000), ordered by member similarity (Goldstone & Kersten, 2003).
  • Natural kinds: occur in the world, members share important features (flowers); labelled only after discovery (Medin & Heit, 1999).
  • Artifacts: invented for a function (tools, sports, furniture); members share fewer basic features (soccer vs cross-country).
  • Ad hoc categories (Barsalou, 1983): formed ‘on the fly’ for a goal (‘things to take on vacation’); low similarity, yet consistent across people.
  • Metaphorical concepts are least coherent: an ‘emotional prison’ (job, relationship, secret) shares only an underlying theme.
🪝 Memory hook: From flowers to metaphors 🌸→⛓️: the further right, the less members look alike.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Categories differ in coherence, from natural kinds (high similarity) to metaphorical concepts (only a shared theme).
Tap to open ▸
Roses and daisies obviously belong together. Soccer and cross-country less so. Suitcases and books only belong together if you’re packing. And an ‘emotional prison’ is held together by an idea, not by looks.
TypeHeld together byExample
Natural kindshared natural featuresflower: rose, daisy
Artifactdesigned functionsport: soccer, cross-country
Ad hoca current goalthings to take on vacation
Metaphoricalan abstract themean emotional prison
▶ semantic network spreading activation Collins Loftus▶ Robinson-Riegler concepts categories▶ ad hoc categories Barsalou(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What makes ad hoc categories special?

They are formed on the fly to serve a goal; members are dissimilar, yet responses are consistent within a culture and typicality still varies.

Order the four types by member similarity.

Natural kinds > artifacts > ad hoc categories > metaphorical concepts.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 19 of 34 · objectives B2 · A3

📐 Similarity-based categorisation and the classical view

Three standards, and three problems for definitions

❓ This lecture answers: How do we decide where a new object belongs by comparing it to a stored standard, and why do definitions fail?
↳ How it fits: This opens Part B’s second question: categorising means judging similarity, and the classical definition view cannot explain games or typicality.
  • Similarity-based approaches: categorisation = judging similarity between the target and a standard in long-term memory; the standard can be defining features, a best example or all members.
  • Classical view (Bruner, Goodnow & Austin, 1956): features are necessary and sufficient (triangle); it counts as similarity based (features matched to the definition).
  • Problem 1: many concepts can’t be specified by necessary and sufficient features (game: Monopoly, dodge ball, hopscotch).
  • Problem 2: it can’t explain graded structure (the typicality effect): asked for furniture, most say table, chair, couch; even ad hoc categories vary (swimsuit vs deck of cards; Rosch, 1973; Rosch & Mervis, 1975).
  • Problem 3: it implies clear-cut boundaries, but categories are fuzzy: is bowling a game or a sport? Students always split.
🪝 Memory hook: Classical view fails the 3 Gs: Games, Grades, Grey zones 🎲📊🌫️.
★ KEY INSIGHT · All three approaches compare items to a stored standard; the classical standard (a definition) fails on definability, typicality and fuzzy boundaries.
Tap to open ▸
Try defining ‘game’ so it covers chess, tag and hopscotch but nothing else: you can’t. And people agree tables are ‘more furniture’ than lamps, and argue about bowling. A strict definition explains none of this.
ProblemExampleWhy the classical view fails
No definitionsgame (Monopoly, dodge ball, hopscotch)no necessary and sufficient set exists
Typicality effecttable, chair, couch named firstall members should be equal
Fuzzy boundariesbowling: game or sport?membership must be all-or-none
▶ semantic network spreading activation Collins Loftus▶ Robinson-Riegler concepts categories▶ classical view problems game Wittgenstein(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is the classical view called similarity based?

Categorisation depends on whether an item’s features are similar to (match) the defining features.

What is the typicality effect, in Robinson-Riegler’s words?

The graded structure of categories: some members (table, chair) are more ‘furniturey’ than others, and people agree strongly on this.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 20 of 34 · objectives A2 · A4 · B2

🔵 The prototype approach

Family resemblance and Posner, Goldsmith & Welton (1967)

❓ This lecture answers: Can comparing a new object to the category’s best example, its prototype, explain how we categorise?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L19: prototypes fix the definition problems, and people even ‘recognise’ a dot-pattern prototype they never saw, suggesting they built a summary.
  • Instead of necessary features, members are likely to have certain features; classification is by resemblance to other members.
  • High family resemblance → typical → serves as the standard (prototype). Robin has all four typical bird features (flies, chirps, feathers, beak); penguin only two.
  • It solves the classical problems: no definition needed; typicality is its basis; bowling lies about equidistant between the game and sport prototypes.
  • Posner, Goldsmith & Welton (1967): after seeing only distortions of a dot-pattern prototype, people confidently ‘recognised’ the never-seen prototype, later as well as patterns shown throughout.
  • Prototypes (as members) are accessed and learned faster and are more easily primed by the category name: short distance to the label in the network.
🪝 Memory hook: The prototype is the face in the family photo 📸 that looks like everyone.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Prototypes are abstracted from experience, and graded similarity to them explains typicality and fuzzy boundaries.
Tap to open ▸
Show people lots of slightly messed-up versions of a dot pattern, never the original, and later they swear they saw the original. Their brain averaged the versions into a prototype.
📄 Posner, Goldsmith & Welton (1967)
ElementDetail
QuestionDo people abstract a prototype from examples?
MethodParticipants saw dot patterns that were statistically generated distortions of a prototype; the prototype itself was never shown; then old/new recognition
Findingspeople confidently ‘recognised’ the unseen prototype, much more than other new patterns; later it was recognised as well as patterns shown throughout
Conclusionparticipants abstracted the average of the patterns
Why it mattersstrong evidence that prototypes are formed

🧩 Comprehension check

How does the prototype approach handle the bowling problem?

Bowling lies near the boundary, about equidistant from the prototypes of ‘game’ and ‘sport’, so it is hard to classify.

Why is Posner et al.’s result so compelling?

People ‘remembered’ a pattern they had never seen, which only makes sense if they had built an abstract prototype.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 21 of 34 · objectives A3 · B2

🧯 Problems with the prototype approach

Correlated features, context and conceptual combination

❓ This lecture answers: Why does a single average example fall short when context or combined concepts like ‘pet fish’ come into play?
↳ How it fits: This shows the limits of prototypes: our knowledge is richer than an average, since typicality shifts with context and with combinations of concepts.
  • As a descriptive term ‘prototype’ is not in doubt; as a theory of representation it has fared less well.
  • People’s categorical knowledge is richer than an average: they know small birds tend to sing and large birds squawk (Mervis & Rosch, 1981) and use it to classify; an average can’t represent such intercorrelations.
  • Typicality is context sensitive (Roth & Shoben, 1983): ‘musical instrument’ → piano, ‘campfire musical instrument’ → guitar or harmonica.
  • Conceptual combination (Hampton, 1993): ‘pet fish’ → guppy or goldfish, typical of neither ‘pet’ nor ‘fish’.
  • If a category centres on one or a few typical members, it is unclear why context or combination should matter.
🪝 Memory hook: An average loses the packages 📦: it knows ‘small’ and ‘sings’, not ‘small birds sing’.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Prototypes cannot capture feature correlations, context effects or concept combinations.
Tap to open ▸
A prototype is like an average of all birds. But averages forget combinations: you know small birds tweet and big birds squawk. And the ‘best instrument’ changes at a campfire. A single average can’t do that.
ProblemFindingSource
Correlated featuressmall birds sing, large birds squawk; used in classificationMervis & Rosch (1981)
Contextcampfire instrument → guitar, not pianoRoth & Shoben (1983)
Combinationpet fish → guppy, goldfishHampton (1993)
▶ semantic network spreading activation Collins Loftus▶ Robinson-Riegler concepts categories▶ prototype theory problems context pet fish(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why can’t a prototype represent that small birds sing?

An average stores each feature’s frequency separately, not which features occur together.

What does the ‘pet fish’ example show?

The typical member of a combined concept need not be typical of either part, which a prototype per concept can’t predict.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 22 of 34 · objectives A2 · A4 · B2

🎸 The exemplar approach

Specific examples as the standard

❓ This lecture answers: What if we compare new objects to specific remembered examples instead of one average?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L21: exemplars handle context and features that go together, because all the detail about members is kept in memory.
  • Partly in response to prototype problems: categories represented by examples (exemplars); no single representation is abstracted over time.
  • Versions: Brooks (1978), Hintzman (1986), Nosofsky (1984). The extreme version stores every encounter and retrieves one when thinking about the concept (Brooks, 1987).
  • Still similarity based, but the standard is a specific example and depends on circumstances: ‘is an eagle a bird?’ retrieves a large bird of prey (Ross & Spalding, 1994).
  • Handles typicality (most stored birds are robin-like and frequently encoded) and context (December makes ‘Jingle Bells’ the example of a song).
  • Handles correlated features (Malt & Smith, 1984): all information about members is stored, so you can work out that small birds sing.
🪝 Memory hook: Exemplars = your photo album 📸: the right photo comes out for the occasion.
★ KEY INSIGHT · By storing examples rather than an average, the exemplar approach explains typicality, context effects and feature correlations.
Tap to open ▸
Instead of one ‘average guitar’, you keep memories of guitars you’ve met. The situation decides which comes to mind: at a campfire, the beat-up acoustic; in December, ‘Jingle Bells’ is the song you think of.
Prototype problemExemplar solution
Typicalitymost stored examples resemble robins; frequently encoded examples are retrieved
Context (campfire, Christmas)context primes particular exemplars
Correlated featuresevery encounter is stored, so co-occurrence can be read off
Classical problemsno definitions needed; fuzzy boundaries and grading arise from similarity
▶ semantic network spreading activation Collins Loftus▶ Robinson-Riegler concepts categories▶ exemplar theory categorization(YouTube search links)

🧩 Comprehension check

What standard does the exemplar approach use?

A specific stored example of the category, chosen by the circumstances, rather than a generalised representation.

How does the exemplar view explain ‘Jingle Bells’ in December?

Temporal context primes and makes that exemplar especially retrievable.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 23 of 34 · objectives A3

⚖️ Problems with exemplars: both views have merit

Posner again, economy, and Malt (1989)

❓ This lecture answers: If exemplars work so well, why do we still need prototypes, and can both be right?
↳ How it fits: This brings the similarity debate to a verdict: storing everything is uneconomical, so people seem to use exemplars or prototypes depending on circumstances.
  • Sometimes people truly use an abstracted representation built from repeated encounters.
  • Posner et al. (1967) again: the prototype was never shown, so there is no corresponding exemplar; how would you recognise something never encoded?
  • Economy (Komatsu, 1992): storing every encounter with every object ‘strains credulity’; and if only some are stored, what decides which?
  • This echoes the economy problem of the template view of pattern recognition.
  • Malt (1989): people classify by exemplars or prototypes depending on circumstances; the boundary between the theories ‘is definitely fuzzy’.
🪝 Memory hook: Prototype = suitcase 🧳 (light, loses details); exemplars = warehouse 🏭 (complete, expensive).
★ KEY INSIGHT · Neither approach wins outright: prototypes and exemplars are each used, depending on the situation.
Tap to open ▸
If you remembered every chair you ever saw, your head would be a warehouse. And exemplars can’t explain ‘remembering’ a dot pattern you never saw. So the mind probably uses both strategies.
Prototype approachExemplar approach
Strengtheconomy; explains Posner’s unseen prototypecorrelations; context; typicality
Weaknesscorrelations, context, combinationeconomy; never-seen prototype
Verdictboth used, depending on circumstances (Malt, 1989)boundary is fuzzy

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is the Posner result a problem for exemplar theory?

Participants recognised the prototype that was never presented, so no stored exemplar could have been matched.

What is the economy problem?

It is implausible that every encounter with every object is stored; and if only some are, the theory must say which.

Part B · Robinson-Riegler (pp. 198–207)
Lecture 24 of 34 · objectives B2 · A2

🔬 The essentialist approach: concepts as theories

Top-down categorisation and Rips (1989)

❓ This lecture answers: Do we categorise by surface similarity, or by our own theory of what something truly is inside?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L23: Rips’ creature looks like an insect but is still judged a bird, so categorisation goes beyond similarity to beliefs about essence.
  • Similarity-based approaches (classical, prototype, exemplar) are bottom-up: they process the features members possess.
  • Alternative, top-down: categorisation based on a person’s theory of the concept’s essence, what it is at its core, which need not be visible (essentialist approaches; Medin & Ortony, 1989).
  • Implication: categories are not represented only by features, and comparing categories is not a simple similarity judgement.
  • Rips (1989): stories about made-up organisms, e.g. a bird-like creature that toxic chemicals turn insect-like: judged more similar to an insect but still a bird.
  • So similarity is not sufficient: categorisation goes ‘well beyond superficial comparison of perceptual similarity’.
🪝 Memory hook: Similarity looks at the costume 🎭; essentialism checks the passport 🛂.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Categorisation can be driven top-down by beliefs about essences, which can override perceptual similarity.
Tap to open ▸
If a bird got chemically changed until it looked like a bug, you’d say it looks more like a bug, but it’s still really a bird. You’re going by what it is ‘inside’, not by what it looks like.
📄 Rips (1989)

Why are similarity-based approaches called bottom-up?

They start from the particular features possessed by the item and compare them with a stored standard.

What does Rips’ transformed bird show?

That people can judge something more similar to one category (insect) yet assign it to another (bird): categorisation is not just similarity.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 25 of 34 · objectives C1

🧩 Semantic dementia: why it is a window on meaning

Selective, progressive, amodal loss of concepts

❓ This lecture answers: What is semantic dementia, and why does losing concepts tell us how concepts are built?
↳ How it fits: Part C tests the theme in the brain: patients lose meaning across all senses, from specific to general, pointing to one central store of concepts.
  • Semantic memory: ‘our knowledge about objects, facts, and concepts, as well as words and their meaning’ (Bozeat et al.).
  • Semantic dementia (SD): circumscribed temporal lobe atrophy (polar and inferolateral regions) with a very selective impairment of conceptual knowledge, so it is an ideal testing ground.
  • Deficits range from sound recognition to naming from definitions, with strong item consistency across modalities → a degraded central, amodal store (Bozeat et al., 2000; Caramazza et al., 1990).
  • Patients have fluent speech; perception, visuospatial skills, reasoning and everyday memory are relatively spared.
  • Loss runs specific → general: duck → ‘swan’ → ‘bird’ → ‘animal’ over 18 months (Hodges et al., 1995); Warrington (1975) took this as a hierarchically organised semantic memory.
🪝 Memory hook: SD is a photo going out of focus 📷: details blur first, the outline stays.
★ KEY INSIGHT · SD selectively erodes amodal conceptual knowledge from specific to general, which reveals how that knowledge is organised.
Tap to open ▸
In semantic dementia part of the temporal lobe shrinks and the meaning of things fades. People still talk fluently and see normally, but a duck first becomes ‘a swan’, then ‘a bird’, then just ‘an animal’.
FeatureSemantic dementia
Causefocal atrophy of polar and inferolateral temporal lobes (L > R)
Core deficitprogressive loss of conceptual knowledge, all modalities
Languagefluent and well structured, but vocabulary shrinks (anomia, poor comprehension)
Sparedperception, visuospatial skills, non-verbal reasoning, working memory, day-to-day memory
Coursespecific before general (duck → swan → bird → animal)

🧩 Comprehension check

Why is SD especially informative about semantic memory?

Its impairment is very selective, affecting conceptual knowledge while other cognition is relatively spared.

What did Warrington (1975) conclude from SD?

That semantic memory is hierarchically organised (superordinate, basic, exemplar levels), with specific levels lost first.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 26 of 34 · objectives C2 · B1

☁️ Beyond hierarchies: a distributed feature view

Garrard et al. (2001), McRae & Cree (2002), Rogers et al. (2002a)

❓ This lecture answers: Is conceptual knowledge a neat tree of categories, or a web of shared features spread across concepts?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L25: the specific-to-general loss can arise from distributed features alone, with typicality coming from similarity to the category’s centre.
  • Warrington’s hierarchy has intuitive appeal, but categories are messier: graded typicality, unclear or double membership, and some categories are more coherent (vehicles vs household items).
  • Alternative: categories are products of individual representations that share a partially common set of features.
  • Feature-listing databases show higher-order structure emerges from a distributed collage of fine-grained attributes, without coding category membership (Garrard et al., 2001; McRae & Cree, 2002).
  • Rated typicality is predicted by feature similarity to the category centroid (Garrard et al., 2001); a connectionist network with simulated damage reproduces the hierarchical SD effect without a coded hierarchy (Rogers et al., 2002a).
  • Features vary from shared (wings on a duck) to distinctive (a male mallard’s iridescent green feathers); living things have more shared features than artefacts.
🪝 Memory hook: Concepts are mosaics 🧩 that share tiles; the shared tiles hold the picture together.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Category structure and typicality can emerge from overlapping features, with shared features especially common in living things.
Tap to open ▸
Instead of a tidy tree, think of each concept as a bundle of features. Ducks and swans share lots of features, dogs share only a few with them. Categories like ‘bird’ appear automatically from that overlap.

Shared within a categorywings, beak (birds)intermediate categories
Distinctivemallard’s iridescent green headone or a few concepts

🧩 Comprehension check

What three observations argue against a purely hierarchical semantic memory?

Graded typicality, unclear or multiple category membership, and differences in category coherence.

How can a network show a ‘hierarchical’ loss without a hierarchy?

Shared features are supported by many concepts and so are more robust to damage than distinctive ones, producing specific-before-general loss.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 27 of 34 · objectives C2

✏️ Drawing as an assessment of semantics

Advantages, drawbacks and a feature-based scoring scheme

❓ This lecture answers: Why use drawing to test what someone still knows about an object, and how can it be scored fairly?
↳ How it fits: This adds a new, non-verbal window on concepts: scoring which features appear in a drawing measures meaning while limiting the effect of drawing talent.
  • Bozeat et al. add drawing as another line of evidence on the structure of conceptual knowledge.
  • Drawing is a non-verbal counterpart to feature listing: it avoids anomia, is easy to administer, needs no complex instructions and yields rich data.
  • Drawbacks: people differ in premorbid drawing skill, and the standard ‘how good is this drawing?’ rating is biased by skill and ignores content.
  • Solution: feature-based scoring (improving Lambon Ralph et al., 1998): controls’ drawings define target features; patient drawings are scored on how many are present.
  • This gives a relatively objective score focused on content that minimises the influence of drawing skill.
🪝 Memory hook: Score the ingredients 🧾, not the artistry 🎨.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Feature-based scoring turns drawings into an objective, content-focused measure of conceptual knowledge.
Tap to open ▸
Instead of asking ‘is this a nice duck?’, the researchers checked which duck parts were there: body, head, two legs, webbed feet, beak, wings. That way a bad artist who knows ducks still scores well.
Drawing assessment
Pronon-verbal output; avoids anomia
Proeasy, no complex instructions, rich data
Conpremorbid drawing skill varies
Conquality ratings biased by skill, ignore content

Why not simply rate how good a drawing is?

Ratings are influenced by drawing skill and do not allow detailed analysis of the content.

Which features counted as targets in Study 1?

Features present in six or more of the eight control drawings of that item.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 28 of 34 · objectives C1 · C2

📋 Study 1: method

Six patients, 64 concepts, a full test battery

❓ This lecture answers: How was Study 1 set up to compare patients’ drawings with their naming and understanding?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L27: the same 64 items appear in every test, so drawing can be compared directly with naming, matching and other measures of meaning.
  • Controls: 8 healthy adults (5 men, 3 women, 55–73 years) drew the 64 items from their names, 1 minute each, ‘not assessed for artistic ability’.
  • Patients: 6 SD patients (DM, MB, KH, GC, JH, FM; 57–61 years), fluent speech with progressive vocabulary loss, focal temporal atrophy on MRI (L > R).
  • General tests: MMSE, letter fluency (F, A, S) ‘to test executive function’, Raven’s matrices, Rey figure copy and recall, VOSP perception subtests.
  • Semantic battery on the same 64 items: category fluency, naming, word–picture matching (9 within-category foils), Pyramids and Palm Trees.
  • Patients drew all 64 items from their names (unlimited time, living and non-living alternated, a fresh sheet each time to avoid perseveration).
🪝 Memory hook: Same 64 items for every test 🔁: so drawing can be compared with naming item by item.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Using the same items across semantic and non-semantic tests lets drawing be compared directly with other measures.
Tap to open ▸
The researchers tested six patients with lots of tasks, some about meaning (naming pictures, matching words) and some not (copying a complex figure, solving puzzles). Then the patients drew 64 things from their names.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 29 of 34 · objectives C1 · C2

📊 Study 1 results: drawing tracks meaning

Correlations of .96–.99 with naming and comprehension

❓ This lecture answers: Do patients’ drawings get worse in step with their loss of meaning, while other skills stay intact?
↳ How it fits: This shows that drawing tracks the loss of concepts almost perfectly, while perception and copying stay largely spared, so the damage is to meaning itself.
  • Patients spanned mild (DM) to severe (FM): MMSE 29 → 8; naming 61 → 0 of 64; word–picture matching 63 → 16 (controls 62.3 and 63.7).
  • Letter fluency was low in all but DM, but ‘most likely’ reflects anomia, not executive dysfunction. Raven’s, Rey copy and VOSP (even object decision) were largely preserved.
  • Drawing correlated with naming and word–picture matching at r = .96–.99 (Spearman, p < .001): one central semantic impairment.
  • Patients drew fewer target features: 0.53 vs 0.95 (Mann–Whitney U = 1.5, p < .01); inter-rater κ = .42 (patients), .48 (controls).
  • Trend for better drawings of familiar items (t = 1.78, p = .07); only KH showed a domain effect (better for man-made items).
🪝 Memory hook: Red falls, teal stays 📉📏: meaning goes, copying skills remain.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Drawing declines in lockstep with other semantic tasks while non-semantic skills are spared: a single, selective conceptual deficit.
Tap to open ▸
As the disease gets worse, patients name fewer pictures and draw worse, and these go down together almost perfectly. But they can still copy a complicated figure. So bad drawing comes from lost meaning, not bad hands or eyes.

What does r = .96–.99 between drawing, naming and matching suggest?

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 30 of 34 · objectives C2

🦆 A duck with four legs: the error patterns

Living things drift to the prototype; artefacts turn into boxes

❓ This lecture answers: What kinds of mistakes appear in patients’ drawings, and why do ducks gain four legs?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L29: distinctive features vanish first and shared features survive or creep in, so concepts slide toward the typical member.
  • Five patients drew some items recognisable as other items, mostly semantically related (watering can → hose; kangaroo → giraffe); cross-domain errors were extremely rare.
  • Living things: loss of distinctive features plus a pull toward a familiar, prototypical animal; incorrect features were added (four legs on a duck).
  • Artefacts: similar loss of distinctive features, but intrusions were very rare; drawings became simpler and box-like (Figure 1, JH’s lamp).
  • Interpretation: shared features are preserved, distinctive ones vulnerable; since living things have more shared features, they drift toward the prototype.
  • Largely shared features (four legs for animals) intrude into concepts that lack them (duck); this parallels naming errors (Hodges et al., 1995).
🪝 Memory hook: Animals melt into ‘generic animal’ 🐾; objects shrink into a box 📦.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Errors are structured: distinctive features are lost and shared features intrude, producing prototypical animals and box-like artefacts.
Tap to open ▸
When the details of ‘duck’ are gone, the patient falls back on what most animals have, so the duck gets four legs. For a lamp, there’s no common ‘object shape’ to fall back on, so it just becomes a box.

Why did patients add four legs to a duck?

‘Four legs’ is a feature shared by many animals; shared features are robust and intrude into concepts that don’t have them.

Why do artefact drawings become box-like rather than gaining intrusions?

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 31 of 34 · objectives C2

🧪 Study 2: copying, delayed copying, drawing to name

Separating perception, memory and meaning

❓ This lecture answers: How can copying a picture, copying it after a short delay, and drawing from a name separate seeing, memory and meaning?
↳ How it fits: This sharpens the test: three tasks need increasing amounts of conceptual knowledge, so the pattern of errors can show where the damage lies.
  • Study 1 relied on verbal input (the spoken name), and some patients refused unknown names; Study 2 added two non-verbal conditions.
  • Immediate copy (picture in sight): visual, spatial and constructional skills, little or no semantics. Delayed copy: count to 15 (≈ 10 s; piloted with DS) → partly conceptual. Drawing to name: most conceptual; non-perceptual prompts (‘a bird that swims on ponds, waddles on land, lays eggs’).
  • 3 patients: DS (mild), DC (moderate), IF (severe), plus 4 matched controls; all 64 items in all three conditions on separate occasions.
  • Scoring by features and modifiers (neck: curved, thin, long, short); target features = drawn by all controls; each feature scored correct, omission or intrusion.
  • Fruit excluded (IF did not draw all eight); a control task of delayed copying of meaningless geometric shapes (3–8 features) tested episodic memory.
🪝 Memory hook: Three doors 🚪🚪🚪: look-and-copy, remember-and-copy, imagine-and-draw.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Graded reliance on semantics across conditions lets the authors isolate the conceptual contribution to drawing.
Tap to open ▸
By comparing copying with the picture in view, copying after 10 seconds and drawing from the word alone, you can see exactly when meaning is needed. If drawings fall apart only when meaning is needed, the problem is meaning.

Why was a 10-second delay chosen?

In piloting with DS, conceptual knowledge already influenced delayed copying after only 10 s.

What is the difference between an omission and an intrusion?

An omission is a target feature (drawn by all controls) left out; an intrusion is an incorrect feature added, like four legs on a duck.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 32 of 34 · objectives C2

📈 Study 2 results: task, severity and domain

Omissions are domain-free; intrusions favour animals

❓ This lecture answers: How do drawing errors change with the task, the patient’s severity and living versus non-living things?
↳ How it fits: Builds on L31: errors grow as tasks rely more on meaning and as illness worsens; missing features appear everywhere, added features mostly in animals.
  • Total errors: main effects of task (F(2,425) = 96.5) and patient (F = 49.5) and an interaction (F = 8.55), all p < .001.
  • Order: immediate copy < delayed copy < drawing to name; and DS < DC < IF: performance worsens with semantic demand and with severity; the task gap widens as semantics degrades.
  • Omissions: effects of patient (F = 62.71) and task (F = 129.41), but no domain effect (F(1,433) = 1.63, n.s.).
  • Intrusions: effects of patient, task and domain: animals had more intrusions than artefacts (F(1,433) = 55.6); very few intrusions in immediate copying.
  • Delayed copying and drawing from name produced similar intrusion rates (p > .1); the task differences again grew with semantic deficit.
🪝 Memory hook: Omissions everywhere ✂️, intrusions mostly in animals 🐾.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Drawing errors scale with semantic demand and severity; intrusions, unlike omissions, are more frequent for animals.

The more a drawing needs meaning, and the sicker the patient, the more mistakes. Leaving things out happens equally for animals and objects, but adding wrong parts happens mostly for animals.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 33 of 34 · objectives C2

🎯 Feature distinctiveness explains the errors

Omissions, intrusions and the vanishing domain effect

❓ This lecture answers: Can how distinctive or widely shared a feature is explain which details get lost or wrongly added?
↳ How it fits: This explains the errors in L30 and L32: once distinctiveness is taken into account, the difference between animals and objects disappears.
  • Each feature got a distinctiveness score: the proportion of items in the same category that also have it (wings on 6 of 8 birds = 0.75); below 0.5 = distinctive.
  • Three classes: shared-by-domain (eyes in most animals), shared-by-category (wings in most birds), distinctive. Animals had more shared features (0.59 per item) than artefacts (0.29).
  • Omissions: distinctive features omitted most (F(2,222) = 186.23), category-shared more than domain-shared; the effect was small in immediate copying.
  • Intrusions: domain-shared features intruded most, then category-shared, then distinctive (F(2,32) = 19.12).
  • With distinctiveness in the model, the animal–artefact difference in intrusions disappeared (F(1,33) = 2.94, p > .1): the ‘domain effect’ is really a feature-distribution effect.
🪝 Memory hook: Common features are the sturdy foundation 🧱; distinctive ones are the decoration 🎀.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Feature distinctiveness, not living vs non-living as such, predicts which features are lost and which intrude.
Tap to open ▸
Features that many things share are like well-worn paths: they survive the disease and even get used where they don’t belong. Features that only one thing has are fragile and vanish first.

Part C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
Lecture 34 of 34 · objectives C2

🏛️ Discussion: a unitary, distributed, amodal system

Controls, consistency and the rival account

❓ This lecture answers: What do the drawing studies conclude about how concepts are stored, and is there a rival explanation?
↳ How it fits: This completes Part C: one shared, feature-based store of meaning, used by drawing, naming and matching, best explains what is lost.
  • Geometric shapes: all patients were within the control range for delayed copying of meaningless figures (only slightly low on difficult ones), so poor delayed copying of objects is semantic, not episodic.
  • Consistency of performance: drawing, naming and matching all depend on the same conceptual knowledge; copying and novel figures (including the Rey figure) were spared.
  • Consistency of errors: like naming, definitions and sorting, drawing loses specific details and keeps domain generalities; intrusions parallel over-extended names for typical items.
  • Rival: a separate structural description system (Riddoch et al., 1988) also damaged. Not refutable, but it can’t explain correlations with verbal tasks or the distinctiveness pattern; preferred: visual representations depend on semantic feedback.
  • Conclusion: a unitary (but very distributed) amodal conceptual network; drawing is a rich, quick, non-verbal assessment, though it says nothing about use or location.
🪝 Memory hook: One shared library 📚 for words and pictures: when the books fade, every reader suffers.
★ KEY INSIGHT · SD supports a single, distributed, amodal semantic system in which shared features are robust and visual knowledge depends on semantic feedback.
Tap to open ▸
Because drawing, naming and understanding words all fail together, and fail in the same way, the brain seems to have one meaning system for everything. The patients can still remember meaningless shapes, so it isn’t their memory for pictures that broke.

What does the geometric-shape control rule out?

Why do the authors prefer a single semantic system over a separate structural description system?
