Warm-up · Scattergories
🧠 In-depth question · Warm-up

How does semantic memory help you win Scattergories?

❓ Canvas question Warm-up, word for word
Warm-up
Je gaat een vereenvoudigde versie van het spel scattergories spelen. […] Je tutor heeft een lijst van zes categorieën. Voorbeelden van deze categorieën kunnen zijn: “vissen”, “groenten” en “muziekgenre”. Daarnaast kiest je tutor ook een letter van het alfabet. […] Het doel is om voor elk van de zes categorieën een voorbeeld op te schrijven dat begint met de gekozen letter. […] Als je antwoord correct is en niemand anders hetzelfde antwoord heeft gegeven, krijg je een punt. […] Na het spel geeft iedereen, behalve de Scattergories Master, aan hoe kennis over het semantisch geheugen gebruikt kan worden om het spel te winnen.

🇬🇧 In English: Play a simplified Scattergories: six categories (e.g. fish, vegetables, music genre), one letter, one minute to write one example per category starting with that letter. A correct answer nobody else gave scores a point; wrong answers (calling a kiwi a vegetable) or shared answers score nothing. Afterwards: how can knowledge about semantic memory help you win?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA game where you must produce category members under a letter constraint, fast and unique.
DiagnosisCategory retrieval (spreading activation, typicality), the letter rule (executive control) and fuzzy boundaries (correct or not?).
TreatmentMap each rule of the game onto a concept from this theme, then turn each into a tip.
  • The category cue spreads activation to its members, strongest for typical ones (salmon, tuna for fish): they come first.
  • But typical answers are the ones everybody writes, so they score nothing: aim for less typical or subordinate/expert members.
  • The lexicon is organised by meaning, not first letter, so the letter filter needs controlled, executive search (sub-cues ka-, ki-, ko-), like the FAS test in Bron C5.
  • Fuzzy boundaries cost points: check borderline items (is a kiwi a vegetable? is a tomato?).
  • Use your network: ad hoc routes (‘fish at the fish market’) and related links reach members the category cue alone misses.
🪝 Memory hook: Typical = shared = zero points 0️⃣; atypical = unique = point ✅.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Scattergories rewards answers that are correct but not typical, while your semantic network is built to hand you the typical ones first: knowing that lets you deliberately search past the prototype.
Tap to open ▸

Scattergories pits two systems against each other. The category name (e.g. fish) activates its node, and activation spreads fastest to the most strongly linked, typical members (salmon, tuna, carp), so these come to mind first (typicality effect; Collins & Loftus, 1975). Because everyone’s network works this way, typical answers are likely to be duplicated and score nothing, so a good strategy is to go deliberately for atypical, subordinate or expert-level members (Tanaka & Taylor, 1991).

The letter constraint does not match how the lexicon is organised (by meaning, not first letter), so you need controlled, executive retrieval: keep the rule in mind, generate sub-cues (ka-, ke-, ki-), inhibit wrong-letter answers and switch strategy when stuck, as in the FAS fluency test. Finally, categories have fuzzy boundaries (Hampton, 1979), so check borderline answers (a kiwi is not a vegetable) and use ad hoc or contextual routes (‘things at the fish market’) to reach members the category cue alone does not activate.

Play a round: press start, then type one answer per category that starts with the letter. Afterwards, compare with the “typical” answers to see whether yours would be unique.

  • Only saying ‘know many words’: link each tip to a concept (typicality, spreading activation, fuzzy boundaries, executive control).
  • Forgetting why typical answers are risky: they are the shared, high-frequency answers.

Bron A · Murphy
🧠 In-depth question · A1

Where did semantics influence cognition earlier in the course?

❓ Canvas question A1, word for word
A1
Deze bron gaat over semantiek: de betekenis van woorden en zinnen. We kwamen semantiek al eerder tegen. Weet je nog waar en hoe semantiek een invloed uitoefende?

🇬🇧 In English: This source is about semantics: the meaning of words and sentences. We met semantics earlier. Do you remember where and how semantics had an influence?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Where did meaning matter before?’ A link-back question to Problems 1–3.
DiagnosisTop-down influence of meaning in attention, short-term/working memory and autobiographical memory/amnesia.
TreatmentName at least two earlier problems, say HOW meaning acted in each, and link to thresholds and activation.
  • Attention: meaning breaks through the filter (your own name, a story switching ears); Treisman’s attenuation theory uses dictionary units with lowered thresholds.
  • STM / working memory: meaning affects coding and forgetting, e.g. release from proactive interference when the semantic category changes. Check against your Problem 2 notes.
  • Autobiographical memory / amnesia: personal semantic facts vs episodic events; semantic knowledge often spared while new episodic learning fails.
  • In each case meaning acts top-down: it shapes what we attend to, store and retrieve.
  • Link: Treisman’s thresholds foreshadow Collins & Loftus’s nodes that fire past a threshold.
🪝 Memory hook: Meaning has been the hidden hand 🫳 in every earlier problem.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Meaning keeps sneaking into processes that look ‘mechanical’: your name grabs attention, word categories change what you forget, and facts about your own life survive amnesia.
Tap to open ▸

Semantics has already appeared in at least three places. In attention, the meaning of an unattended message can break through the filter, for example your own name (cocktail-party effect) or a story that switches ears; Treisman explained this with dictionary units whose thresholds are lowered for meaningful or expected words. In short-term and working memory, meaning influences coding and forgetting (e.g. release from proactive interference when the semantic category changes). In autobiographical memory and amnesia, semantic knowledge about ourselves is distinguished from episodic memories of events, and semantic memory can be preserved when episodic memory is impaired.

In each case meaning acts top-down: what something means shapes what we attend to, store and retrieve. Treisman’s thresholds foreshadow the threshold-based activation in semantic network models (Collins & Loftus, 1975).

  • Naming only one example: give at least two problems and say *how* meaning had an effect.
  • Saying ‘semantics = memory’: semantics is meaning; semantic memory is one store of it.
  • Missing the link to this week’s thresholds and activation.

Bron A · Murphy
🧠 In-depth question · A2

Does typicality affect how we generalise?

❓ Canvas question A2, word for word
A2
Concepten laten je toe om dingen die je leerde over een beperkt aantal items te generaliseren naar een veel grotere set van items. Als je bijvoorbeeld leert dat mussen en roodborstjes een bepaalde eigenschap hebben, dan ben je geneigd om te veronderstellen dat alle vogels die eigenschap delen. Denk je dat typicaliteit het generalisatiepatroon beïnvloedt?

🇬🇧 In English: Concepts let you generalise what you learned about a limited number of items to a much larger set. If you learn that sparrows and robins have a certain property, you tend to assume all birds share it. Do you think typicality influences the pattern of generalisation?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Does typicality change how far a fact spreads?’
DiagnosisConcepts support generalisation (Murphy); typicality = family resemblance; prototype and exemplar views.
TreatmentPredict: typical premises generalise further; explain WHY via feature overlap; add the atypical contrast and a caution.
  • Generalising from a few members to the category (category-based induction) is a core function of concepts (Murphy).
  • Typical members (sparrow, robin) share many features with most birds, so a property they have probably reflects what birds share → strong generalisation.
  • Atypical members (penguin, ostrich) have unusual features; their property may be tied to those, so people generalise less.
  • Prototype view: typical items are close to the summary and ‘stand for’ the category; exemplar view: they resemble many stored birds.
  • background premise typicality and diversity effects (Rips, 1975; Osherson et al., 1990); risk: stereotypes from ‘typical’ group members.
🪝 Memory hook: Robin facts fly far 🐦→🐦🐦🐦; penguin facts stay home 🐧.
★ KEY INSIGHT · If robins and sparrows turn out to have some new property, you’d bet most birds do. If only penguins have it, you’d think it’s a penguin quirk.
Tap to open ▸

Yes: typicality strengthens generalisation. Because typical members such as sparrows and robins share many features with other birds (family resemblance; Rosch & Mervis, 1975), a property they have is likely to reflect what birds in general are like, so we readily extend it to all birds. A property learned about atypical members such as penguins may be tied to their unusual features, so we generalise it less confidently.

In prototype terms, typical members are close to the category summary and therefore represent the category well; in exemplar terms, they resemble many stored exemplars, so the property spreads widely. This mirrors Murphy’s Text Box 1, in which typicality influences learning, categorisation and reasoning. A caution: generalising from salient or ‘typical’ members can lead to over-generalisation, as in stereotypes.

  • Saying ‘typical = more generalisation’ without the *why* (feature overlap / representativeness).
  • Forgetting the atypical contrast.
  • Presenting premise typicality or diversity effects as coming from the readings: they are background.

Bron A · Murphy
🧠 In-depth question · A3

Why is it called family resemblance?

❓ Canvas question A3, word for word
A3
Verklaar de family resemblance in de naam family resemblance theory.

🇬🇧 In English: Explain the ‘family resemblance’ in the name family resemblance theory.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Why that name?’ An explain-the-metaphor question.
DiagnosisRosch & Mervis (1975); the classical view it replaces; Wittgenstein’s games (background).
TreatmentDescribe a real family (overlapping features, none shared by all), map it onto categories, then link to typicality.
  • In a family, members resemble each other through overlapping, criss-crossing features (nose, eyes, hair), yet no single feature is shared by everyone.
  • Rosch & Mervis (1975): categories work the same way: members share features with some others, not a set common to all, so there is no definition.
  • background the term comes from Wittgenstein (1953) and his ‘games’ example, the same example Robinson-Riegler uses.
  • Typicality follows: the more features an item shares with other members (and the fewer with other categories), the more it ‘looks like the family’.
  • Robinson-Riegler: high family resemblance = typical member = the prototype.
🪝 Memory hook: Dad’s nose, Mum’s eyes 👃👀: everyone looks related, nobody has everything.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Look at a family photo: you can tell they’re related, but there isn’t one thing they all have. Categories like ‘game’ or ‘bird’ hang together the same way.
Tap to open ▸

The theory is named after the way members of a family resemble each other: relatives look alike because they share overlapping features (one has the father’s nose, another the mother’s eyes) yet no single feature is shared by all of them. Rosch and Mervis (1975) proposed that categories are structured in the same way: members are held together by a network of overlapping features rather than by a defining set that all members possess (the term goes back to Wittgenstein’s analysis of ‘games’).

An item’s typicality is its degree of family resemblance: how many features it shares with other members and how few with other categories. So a robin is a better ‘family member’ of the birds than a penguin, which shares few bird features and some fish features.

  • Describing typicality without explaining the *name*.
  • Implying members share one common feature: the point is that none is shared by all.

Bron A · Murphy
🧠 In-depth question · A4

Where have we met a hierarchical organisation before?

❓ Canvas question A4, word for word
A4
De tekst van Murphy stelt dat veel categorieën hiërarchisch zijn georganiseerd. We zijn eerder zo'n hiërarchische organisatie van informatie tegengekomen. Weet je nog waar?

🇬🇧 In English: Murphy’s text states that many categories are hierarchically organised. We came across such a hierarchical organisation of information earlier. Do you remember where?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Where have we seen general → specific levels before?’
DiagnosisMurphy’s superordinate–basic–subordinate levels; Conway’s autobiographical knowledge base (Problem 3a).
TreatmentName the earlier model, map its levels onto Murphy’s, and note the preferred middle level in both.
  • Autobiographical memory (Problem 3a): Conway’s knowledge base: lifetime periods → general events → event-specific knowledge.
  • Parallel: superordinate ↔ lifetime period; basic ↔ general event; subordinate ↔ event-specific knowledge.
  • In both, a middle level is the preferred entry point (general events; the basic level).
  • Within this theme: Collins & Quillian’s hierarchical network background and Warrington’s (1975) hierarchical view in SD (duck → bird → animal).
  • Also possible, depending on your notes: hierarchical chunking in STM.
🪝 Memory hook: Life story and categories are both Russian dolls 🪆 with a favourite middle doll.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Your memories are organised like categories: big chapters of life, typical events inside them, and specific details inside those, just like animal → bird → robin.
Tap to open ▸

We met a hierarchical organisation in autobiographical memory. Conway’s autobiographical knowledge base is organised from general to specific: lifetime periods (‘when I lived in Rotterdam’) contain general events (‘evenings at the library’), which contain event-specific knowledge (sensory details of one evening). This parallels Murphy’s category hierarchy of superordinate, basic and subordinate levels, and in both cases an intermediate level (general events; the basic level) is especially accessible.

Within this week’s readings, hierarchies also appear in network models of semantic memory and in the specific-to-general loss in semantic dementia (duck → swan → bird → animal; Warrington, 1975; Hodges et al., 1995).

  • Naming the earlier model without mapping its levels onto Murphy’s.
  • Forgetting the key parallel: general → specific with a preferred middle level.

Bron A · Murphy
🧠 In-depth question · A5

How are prototypes and definitions different?

❓ Canvas question A5, word for word
A5
Waarin verschillen prototypes en definities?

🇬🇧 In English: How do prototypes and definitions differ?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Compare two representations.’
DiagnosisClassical view (necessary and sufficient features) vs prototype view (weighted features, graded similarity).
TreatmentBuild a comparison table: what is stored, membership, typicality, boundaries, origin, scope.
  • A definition lists necessary and jointly sufficient features: tick every box or you are out.
  • A prototype is a summary of characteristic features weighted by frequency; no single feature is required (a penguin doesn’t fly but is a bird).
  • Definitions → all-or-none membership, equal members, sharp boundaries. Prototypes → graded similarity, typicality, fuzzy boundaries (bowling).
  • Prototypes are abstracted from experience and can be a never-seen average (Posner et al., 1967).
  • Definitions suit formal concepts (triangle); most natural categories have prototypes but no definitions.
🪝 Memory hook: Definition = checklist ✅; prototype = bullseye 🎯.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A definition is like an exam with a pass mark of 100%: miss one requirement and you fail. A prototype is like a target: the closer to the centre, the better the example, and the edge is blurry.
Tap to open ▸
DimensionDefinition (classical view)Prototype
What is storednecessary and jointly sufficient featuressummary of characteristic features, weighted by frequency
Every feature required?yesno (a penguin doesn’t fly but is still a bird)
Membershipall-or-nonegraded: similarity to the prototype
Typicalityall members equal: cannot explain itbuilt in: closer = more typical
Boundariessharpfuzzy (bowling between sport and game)
Origincan be stated or taughtabstracted from experience; can be never seen (Posner et al., 1967)
Works forformal concepts (triangle, prime number)natural and everyday categories (bird, furniture, game)

A definition specifies necessary and jointly sufficient features: anything that has them all is a member, anything that lacks one is not, so membership is all-or-none, all members are equally good and boundaries are sharp. A prototype is a summary of the features members tend to have, weighted by how common they are; no single feature is required. Membership is graded by similarity to the prototype, which explains typicality (robins match better than penguins) and fuzzy boundaries. Definitions suit formal concepts such as ‘triangle’, whereas most natural categories cannot be defined but do have prototypes, abstracted from experience (Posner et al., 1967).

  • Saying a prototype is ‘one real member’: it can be an abstract average.
  • Listing differences without linking them to typicality and fuzzy boundaries.

Bron A · Murphy
🧠 In-depth question · A6

How is essentialism related to the classical view?

❓ Canvas question A6, word for word
A6
In welke zin zijn psychologisch essentialisme en de klassieke visie op concepten en categorieën gerelateerd?

🇬🇧 In English: In what sense are psychological essentialism and the classical view of concepts and categories related?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘How are two ideas related?’ Needs similarities AND differences.
DiagnosisClassical view (defining features) vs essentialism (hidden causal essence; Keil, 1989).
TreatmentGive two similarities (defining core, all-or-none) and three differences (hidden vs visible, causal, natural kinds only); add Keil.
  • Similarity 1: both assume a core that all and only members possess (defining features vs essence).
  • Similarity 2: both imply all-or-none membership: ‘in or out, no in-between’ is Murphy’s first sign of essentialism.
  • Difference 1: the classical core is visible features; the essence is hidden, often unknown, and causes the visible features.
  • Difference 2: surface features can vary or mislead without changing membership (Keil’s raccoon looking like a skunk).
  • Difference 3: essentialism applies mainly to natural kinds, not artifacts (coffeepot → bird feeder).
🪝 Memory hook: Classical = the label on the box 🏷️; essentialism = the DNA inside 🧬.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Both ideas say ‘there’s one thing that makes a dog a dog’. The classical view thinks you can see it and list it. Essentialism thinks it’s hidden inside, and the visible stuff is just a clue.
Tap to open ▸

Psychological essentialism can be seen as a psychological descendant of the classical view. Both hold that a category has a core that all and only its members possess, and both imply all-or-none membership with no in-between. The difference lies in where that core is located. The classical view places it in observable defining features used to classify items, whereas essentialism places it in a hidden essence, often unknown to the person, that is believed to cause the observable features.

As a result, surface features can vary or mislead without changing membership: Keil’s (1989) raccoon made to look like a skunk is still judged a raccoon. Essentialism therefore explains why people believe categories are well defined (the outrage over Pluto) even though they cannot give definitions, while everyday identification relies on typical, graded features. It applies mainly to natural kinds, not to artifacts.

  • Saying essentialism *is* the classical view: the essence is hidden and causal, not a list of visible features.
  • Forgetting Keil’s evidence or the natural kind vs artifact contrast.

Bron B · Robinson-Riegler
🧠 In-depth question · B1

Explain the typicality effect with a semantic network

❓ Canvas question B1, word for word
B1
Categorieverificatietaken worden gebruikt om na te gaan hoe we categorielidmaatschap bepalen. In deze taak verifiëren deelnemers zo snel mogelijk eenvoudige stellingen zoals “Een zwaluw (swallow) is een vogel” of “Een kraanvogel (crane) is een vogel”. Hieronder vind je een voorbeeld van een klein semantisch netwerk. Gebruik het om het typicaliteitseffect uit te leggen.

🇬🇧 In English: Category verification tasks are used to examine how we determine category membership. Participants verify simple statements as fast as possible, such as ‘A swallow is a bird’ or ‘A crane is a bird’. Below is an example of a small semantic network. Use it to explain the typicality effect.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA network picture plus a speed difference: ‘explain with the model’.
DiagnosisSpreading activation (Collins & Loftus, 1975): link length = strength; summation; threshold.
TreatmentWalk through the mechanism step by step for swallow vs crane, then contrast with a strict hierarchy.
  • Reading the sentence activates SWALLOW (or CRANE) and BIRD; activation spreads and weakens with distance.
  • Link length reflects associative strength: the typical swallow has a short, strong link to BIRD; the atypical crane a longer, weaker one.
  • SWALLOW shares many feature nodes with BIRD (flies, small, sings) → activation arrives along several paths and sums.
  • Threshold is reached sooner for the swallow → faster ‘true’: that speed difference is the typicality effect.
  • A strict hierarchy (Collins & Quillian background) puts both one link from BIRD → no difference; variable link strengths are needed. Apply the same reasoning to the network in your handout.
🪝 Memory hook: Swallow lives next door to BIRD 🏠; crane lives across town 🚌.
★ KEY INSIGHT · In your head ‘swallow’ is closely tied to ‘bird’, with lots of shared bird features. ‘Crane’ is further away. So ‘a swallow is a bird’ clicks faster.
Tap to open ▸

In a spreading-activation network (Collins & Loftus, 1975), verifying ‘A swallow is a bird’ activates the SWALLOW and BIRD nodes; activation spreads along their links, weakens with distance, and the statement is verified once enough activation accumulates. Typical members like the swallow are connected to BIRD by short, strong links and share many feature nodes with it (flies, small, sings), so activation arrives quickly and along several routes. Atypical members like the crane have longer, weaker links and fewer shared typical features (long legs, wading), so the threshold is reached later.

The result is faster verification for typical members: the typicality effect. Robinson-Riegler puts it as a short distance between category prototypes and the category label. A strictly hierarchical network with equal links could not explain this.

  • Describing the network without the mechanism (spread, decay, summation, threshold).
  • Not saying which link is shorter and why (feature overlap = typicality).

Bron B · Robinson-Riegler
🧠 In-depth question · B2

Is there a typicality-like effect for features?

❓ Canvas question B2, word for word
B2
Eigenschapverificatietaken worden gebruikt om na te gaan hoe eigenschappen van categorieën worden opgeslagen en opgehaald. In deze taak verifiëren deelnemers eenvoudige stellingen zoals “Een kanarie is geel” of “Een kanarie zingt”. Bekijk het semantische netwerk hieronder. Op basis hiervan, denk je dat er zoiets bestaat als een typicaliteitseffect voor eigenschappen?

🇬🇧 In English: Feature verification tasks examine how properties of categories are stored and retrieved: ‘A canary is yellow’, ‘A canary sings’. Look at the semantic network below. Based on it, do you think there is something like a typicality effect for properties?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Is there a typicality effect for features?’ A prediction from the network.
DiagnosisFeature verification; links to features differ in strength (pointy ears vs skin).
TreatmentSay yes, give the mechanism (link strength / proximity), cite the cat example, then apply to yellow vs sings and contrast with a hierarchy.
  • Features are nodes too, linked to concepts with different strengths.
  • Robinson-Riegler: ‘A cat has pointy ears’ is verified faster than ‘A cat has skin’: it shows the proximity of features to the concept.
  • So yes: characteristic, strongly associated features (yellow, sings for a canary) are verified faster than generic or remote ones (has skin, breathes).
  • For your handout: compare the link lengths of ‘yellow’ and ‘sings’: the shorter link predicts the faster response.
  • A strict hierarchy stores both at CANARY → equal times; only ‘has skin’ (at ANIMAL) would be slow.
🪝 Memory hook: Features have favourites too ⭐: ‘pointy ears’ is the robin of cat features.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Some facts about a thing are right on the surface of your mind, like ‘canaries are yellow’; others, like ‘canaries have skin’, are true but buried. The surface ones are checked faster.
Tap to open ▸

Yes. In a spreading-activation network features are linked to concepts with varying strengths, so their verification times should differ just as exemplars do. Features that are characteristic of and strongly associated with a concept (for a canary, being yellow or singing) sit close to the CANARY node and are verified quickly, whereas general or less associated features such as ‘has skin’ are distant and verified slowly. Robinson-Riegler reports exactly this for ‘A cat has pointy ears’ versus ‘A cat has skin’.

Which of ‘yellow’ and ‘sings’ is faster depends on their relative link strengths in the network shown; a strict hierarchical model would predict no difference between them, because both are stored at the canary level.

  • Answering only ‘yes’ without the mechanism (link strength / proximity).
  • Ignoring that hierarchical and spreading-activation networks predict different things.

Bron B · Robinson-Riegler
🧠 In-depth question · B3

Why are correlated features a problem for prototypes?

❓ Canvas question B3, word for word
B3
Er is onderzoek dat aangeeft dat mensen beseffen dat sommige eigenschappen van categorieleden samenhangen: kleine vogels produceren bijvoorbeeld andere geluiden dan grote vogels. Leg uit waarom dit onderzoek problematisch is voor de prototypebenadering.

🇬🇧 In English: Research shows people realise that some properties of category members go together: small birds make different sounds than large birds. Explain why this research is problematic for the prototype approach.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Why is X a problem for theory Y?’
DiagnosisPrototype = single summary of independently weighted features; correlated features (Mervis & Rosch, 1981; Malt & Smith, 1984).
TreatmentExplain what an average stores and what it loses, give the failed prediction, name exemplars as the fix.
  • A prototype is a single summary: each feature gets its own weight (how common it is).
  • If half of birds are small and half sing, it stores ‘small .5’ and ‘sings .5’, but not that the small ones are the singers.
  • So it predicts a small squawking bird is as good a bird as a small singing one; people know better and use correlations when classifying (Mervis & Rosch, 1981).
  • Robinson-Riegler: ‘it’s not clear how an average representation could allow for this’.
  • Exemplars solve it: each stored bird keeps its size and its song together (Malt & Smith, 1984).
🪝 Memory hook: An average makes a smoothie 🥤: you can taste banana and strawberry, but not which came together.
★ KEY INSIGHT · If you only remember the ‘average bird’, you lose combinations: you’d know birds are sometimes small and sometimes sing, but not that it’s the small ones that sing.
Tap to open ▸

The prototype approach represents a category as a single summary of independently weighted features. Such an average records how common each feature is (some birds are small, some sing) but not which features occur together, so the information that small birds tend to sing while large birds squawk is lost. The approach would therefore predict that a small squawking bird matches the prototype as well as a small singing bird, whereas people are sensitive to these correlations and use them in classification (Mervis & Rosch, 1981).

Exemplar theory handles this naturally because each stored exemplar keeps its features together, so correlations can be read off the stored examples (Malt & Smith, 1984). It is one reason Robinson-Riegler concludes that prototypes work better as a description than as an explanation.

  • Saying ‘prototypes can’t handle variation’: the specific problem is co-occurrence between features.
  • Not naming the alternative that solves it (exemplars).

Bron B · Robinson-Riegler
🧠 In-depth question · B4

Spreading activation in everyday algorithms

❓ Canvas question B4, word for word
B4
De nummers die je aanbevolen krijgt op Spotify worden bepaald door een algoritme dat erg lijkt op spreading activation in semantische netwerken. Kun je andere zulke voorbeelden bedenken die jou persoonlijk beïnvloeden? Op wat voor soort data en mechanismen denk je dat deze algoritmes bouwen?

🇬🇧 In English: The songs Spotify recommends are chosen by an algorithm much like spreading activation in semantic networks. Can you think of other such examples that influence you personally? What kinds of data and mechanisms do you think these algorithms build on?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomAn application question: ‘find it in your life, then explain the machinery’.
DiagnosisNodes, links, link strength, spreading activation, threshold, context (priming).
TreatmentGive 3–4 personal examples, then map recommender parts onto network parts; add a critical note.
  • Examples: YouTube ‘Up next’, Netflix rows, TikTok For You, Instagram Explore, Amazon ‘also bought’, search autocomplete, LinkedIn jobs and contacts.
  • Nodes: songs, videos, products, people, jobs, and you.
  • Links from co-occurrence (items used by the same people: collaborative filtering) and from content similarity (genre, tempo, keywords).
  • Your plays, likes, skips, watch time and searches act like a prime; activation spreads and decays; top-scoring items pass the threshold and are shown.
  • Context (time, device, playlist) works like priming; risk: filter bubbles and, in hiring tools, reproducing past biases. Describe mechanisms generally: algorithms are proprietary.
🪝 Memory hook: Your feed is a semantic network that never sleeps 📱.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Every song you play lights up connected songs, the ones lots of similar listeners also played. The most lit-up ones end up in your recommendations.
Tap to open ▸
Semantic network ideaRecommender equivalent
Nodessongs, videos, products, people, jobs, and you
Links and strengthco-occurrence: items used by the same people become strongly linked (collaborative filtering); content similarity links similar items
Activation from the primeplays, likes, searches, clicks, skips, watch time, follows
Spreading with decayfollowing links out from your history; closer items score higher
Threshold / retrievaltop-scoring items are shown
Context effectstime of day, device, location, current playlist (like priming)

Many systems I use work similarly: YouTube and Netflix recommendations, TikTok’s For You page, Amazon’s ‘frequently bought together’, search autocomplete and LinkedIn’s job and contact suggestions. Broadly, they represent items (and users) as nodes and derive link strengths from behavioural data across millions of users, so items consumed by the same people become strongly connected; they also use content features to link similar items. My recent activity acts like a prime: its activation spreads to connected items, weakening with distance, and the highest-scoring items pass the threshold and are recommended. Unlike human semantic memory, these networks are optimised for engagement and can create feedback loops such as filter bubbles.

  • Listing apps without the mechanism (nodes, links from co-occurrence, spread, threshold).
  • Claiming precise knowledge of a company’s proprietary algorithm.

Bron C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
🧠 In-depth question · C1

Apply the SD description to the woman in the video

❓ Canvas question C1, word for word
C1
Semantische dementie is een progressieve ziekte, gekenmerkt door een geleidelijk en selectief verlies van conceptuele kennis, wat resulteert in een beperkte woordenschat tijdens het spreken, moeilijkheden met het begrijpen van wat er gezegd wordt, en problemen met het identificeren van objecten en personen in verschillende modaliteiten. Het algemene intellectuele vermogen, het dagelijkse geheugen en de visueel-perceptuele vaardigheden blijven relatief gespaard. De taal blijft vloeiend en goed gestructureerd. Hoe is deze beschrijving van toepassing op de vrouw in deze video?

🇬🇧 In English: Semantic dementia is a progressive disease with a gradual, selective loss of conceptual knowledge: limited vocabulary in speech, difficulty understanding what is said, and problems identifying objects and people across modalities. General intellect, everyday memory and visuo-perceptual skills stay relatively spared; language stays fluent and well structured. How does this description apply to the woman in the video?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Apply a clinical description to a case.’
DiagnosisThe SD profile: lost (concepts, vocabulary, comprehension, identification) vs spared (intellect, everyday memory, perception, fluency).
TreatmentTick off each element with evidence from the video, then stress the contrast lost vs spared.
  • Look for empty, fluent speech: normal grammar and melody but vague words (‘thing’, ‘that one’).
  • Listen for comprehension failures (‘What’s a …?’) and naming problems: a loss of meaning, not just word-finding.
  • Check other modalities: does she fail to recognise objects, pictures, sounds or people?
  • Note what is spared: following the conversation, recalling recent events, seeing and copying.
  • Conclude with the dissociation, as in Bozeat et al.’s patients who copied the Rey figure but could not name or draw from names. I could not open the video, so complete the guide with your own observations.
🪝 Memory hook: Fluent words, missing meaning 🗣️❓.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Watch for someone who talks smoothly and remembers what she did today, but doesn’t know what some ordinary words or objects are. That mix is semantic dementia.
Tap to open ▸

(Complete with your own observations.) The woman shows the core picture of semantic dementia: her speech is fluent and grammatically well formed, yet empty of specific content: she uses general terms such as [example] and struggles to name [example]. She also seems not to understand some common words, for example [example], which reflects a loss of conceptual knowledge rather than a pure word-finding problem.

By contrast, [example of intact day-to-day memory / reasoning / perception] shows that her general intellect, everyday memory and perception are relatively spared. This dissociation (meaning lost, other cognition intact) is what makes the disorder selective, and it matches Bozeat et al.’s patients, who could copy complex figures but could not name or draw objects from their names.

  • Describing her as ‘forgetful’ in general: SD is a loss of meaning, not of everyday memory.
  • Listing symptoms without evidence from the video.
  • Forgetting the spared abilities: the contrast is the point.

Bron C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
🧠 In-depth question · C2

Feature listing: birds vs furniture

❓ Canvas question C2, word for word
C2
Probeer zelf eens om eigenschappen voor een categorie te genereren. Schrijf elk vijf eigenschappen op van vogels en vijf eigenschappen van meubels. Vergelijk de eigenschappen onderling. Stemmen jullie bevindingen overeen met die van Bozeat et al. (2003)?

🇬🇧 In English: Try generating properties for a category yourself. Each write down five properties of birds and five of furniture. Compare the properties. Do your findings match those of Bozeat et al. (2003)?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA do-it-yourself feature listing, then ‘compare with the paper’.
DiagnosisShared vs distinctive features; living things have more shared features (0.59 vs 0.29).
TreatmentReport what you listed, state the pattern (agreement, shared vs scattered, perceptual vs functional), link to intrusions and box-like drawings, add the level caveat.
  • Typical lists: birds: wings, feathers, beak, lays eggs, flies; furniture: in a house, sit or put things on it, legs, wood, flat surface.
  • Agreement: bird lists overlap strongly; furniture lists vary more.
  • Bird features apply to almost all birds; furniture features to only some items (a lamp or rug has no legs). Bird features are perceptual parts, furniture features mostly functional.
  • Matches Bozeat: animals have more shared features (0.59 vs 0.29 per item) → prototypical animal drawings with intrusions, box-like artefacts.
  • Caveat: furniture is a superordinate (few shared features by nature), while ‘bird’ often acts basic-level.
🪝 Memory hook: Bird lists are clones 🐦🐦; furniture lists are a garage sale 🪑🛋️💡.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Everyone writes wings, feathers, beak for birds. For furniture, people write all sorts of different things, because a lamp, a rug and a bed don’t share much. That’s exactly what Bozeat found.
Tap to open ▸
BirdsFurniture
has wingsused in a house or room
has feathersyou sit, lie on or put things on it
has a beakoften has legs
lays eggsoften made of wood
can fly (most)has a flat surface (many)

Our bird lists overlapped strongly (wings, feathers, beak, lays eggs, flies), and these features apply to almost all birds; our furniture lists varied more and consisted of features that apply only to some items (legs, made of wood, used to sit on). This mirrors Bozeat et al.’s finding that living things have more shared features than artefacts (0.59 vs 0.29 per item). Because shared features are the most robust in semantic dementia and the most likely to intrude, patients’ animal drawings became prototypical (a duck with four legs), while artefact drawings mainly lost distinctive details and became box-like. One caveat: furniture is a superordinate category, which shares few features by nature, so the comparison partly reflects category level.

  • Listing features without drawing the conclusion (shared vs distinctive).
  • Missing the link to intrusions and box-like drawings.
  • Ignoring that furniture is superordinate.

Bron C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
🧠 In-depth question · C3

Which approach best explains the drawings?

❓ Canvas question C3, word for word
C3
Welke benadering van concept-representaties kan de tekenresultaten van de patiënten in Bozeat et al. (2003) het best verklaren?

🇬🇧 In English: Which approach to concept representation can best explain the drawing results of the patients in Bozeat et al. (2003)?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Which theory fits the data best?’ An evaluation question.
DiagnosisClassical, prototype, exemplar, knowledge views vs the findings: distinctive lost first, shared survive and intrude, prototypical animals, within-category errors.
TreatmentList the findings, test each theory against them, pick prototype/feature-based, and name the authors’ distributed network.
  • Facts to explain: distinctive features lost first; shared features kept and intruding; animals drift to a prototype; errors stay within category.
  • Classical: predicts all-or-none loss of defining features; cannot explain graded loss or intrusions ✗.
  • Prototype / family resemblance: the shared, high-weight features are the prototype; as details fade, the drawing collapses toward it ✓.
  • Exemplar: explains substitutions (kangaroo → giraffe) but not domain-level features no specific duck has ±.
  • Authors’ frame: a distributed feature network (Rogers et al., 2002a): the mechanism behind the prototype-like pattern.
🪝 Memory hook: Erosion reveals the skeleton 🦴: what remains is the prototype.
★ KEY INSIGHT · As the disease removes details, every animal drawing slides toward ‘generic animal’. That’s what you’d expect if concepts are bundles of weighted features with the common ones at the core.
Tap to open ▸

The results fit a feature-based, prototype (family-resemblance) view best, implemented as a distributed feature network. Patients lost distinctive features first and kept features shared across a domain; their animal drawings became ‘prototypical’ and gained intruding shared features, such as four legs on a duck. This is what we expect if concepts are sets of weighted, overlapping features: the shared, high-weight features that make up the category’s prototype are the most robust, so as distinctive information fades the representation collapses toward the prototype.

The classical view cannot explain gradual, graded loss or intrusions, and the exemplar view accounts for within-category substitutions but not for domain-level features that no specific exemplar possesses. Bozeat et al. themselves interpret the data as a unitary but highly distributed conceptual network, in which domain differences arise from how features are distributed (Rogers et al., 2002a).

  • Picking a theory without testing it against specific findings.
  • Ignoring the distributed-network interpretation the authors actually favour.

Bron C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
🧠 In-depth question · C4

Why does it matter what drawing does and doesn’t correlate with?

❓ Canvas question C4, word for word
C4
De auteurs van het artikel benadrukken dat de prestatie op de tekentaak correleert met de prestatie op semantische taken, maar niet met de prestatie op bijvoorbeeld het kopiëren van een figuur of intelligentietaken zoals Raven’s matrices. Waarom vinden ze dit zo belangrijk?

🇬🇧 In English: The authors stress that performance on the drawing task correlates with performance on semantic tasks, but not with, for example, copying a figure or intelligence tasks such as Raven’s matrices. Why do they find this so important?

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Why does this pattern matter?’ A logic-of-evidence question.
DiagnosisConvergent (r = .96–.99) and discriminant evidence; dissociation logic; selective, amodal deficit.
TreatmentSay what the correlation rules IN, what the spared tasks rule OUT, then give the three conclusions.
  • Rule in a common cause: drawing correlates with naming and word–picture matching at r = .96–.99: all depend on conceptual knowledge.
  • Rule out alternatives: poor drawing could stem from perception, visuospatial or motor problems, picture memory or general decline, but copying (Rey, immediate), geometric-shape recall and Raven’s are relatively preserved.
  • Conclusion 1: the drawing deficit is genuinely semantic, so drawing is a valid non-verbal semantic test.
  • Conclusion 2: SD is selective, not global dementia, which is why it informs us about semantic memory. Conclusion 3: verbal and non-verbal tasks fail together → a unitary, amodal system.
  • Accuracy note: the paper reports correlations for the semantic tasks; for copying and Raven’s it reports preserved performance, not correlations.
🪝 Memory hook: Correlates with meaning ✅, not with skill ❌ → it’s about meaning.
★ KEY INSIGHT · If bad drawing went together with bad copying or bad puzzle-solving, maybe the patients just can’t draw or think. But it only goes together with naming and understanding words, so it must be about lost meaning.
Tap to open ▸

The pattern pins the drawing impairment on semantic memory specifically. The very high correlations with naming and word–picture matching (r = .96–.99) show that drawing, naming and comprehension share a common cause: the degradation of central conceptual knowledge. The relatively preserved performance on copying the Rey figure, immediate copying and delayed copying of meaningless geometric shapes, and on Raven’s matrices rules out alternative explanations such as visual, visuospatial or motor impairment, a visual episodic memory problem and general intellectual decline.

Together this dissociation shows that poor drawing reflects impoverished concepts, that drawing is a valid non-verbal test of semantic knowledge, and that semantic dementia is a selective disorder. Because verbal and non-verbal semantic tasks decline together, it also supports a unitary, amodal semantic system.

  • Only saying ‘it shows a correlation’: explain what it rules in and what it rules out.
  • Claiming the paper reports zero correlations with copying: it reports preserved performance.

Bron C · Bozeat et al. (2003)
🧠 In-depth question · C5

Why is letter fluency (F, A, S) an executive test?

❓ Canvas question C5, word for word
C5
De patiënten worden onderworpen aan een uitgebreide testbatterij, waarin ze onder meer een verbal fluency test met de letters F, A, en S afleggen. In deze test dienen deelnemers binnen 1 minuut zoveel mogelijk woorden te bedenken die beginnen met de doelletter. Leg uit waarom deze test wordt omschreven als een test voor executief functioneren. (Hint: probleem 2B)

🇬🇧 In English: The patients take an extensive test battery, including a verbal fluency test with the letters F, A and S: produce as many words as possible starting with the target letter within one minute. Explain why this test is described as a test of executive functioning. (Hint: problem 2B)

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
Symptom‘Why does a word test measure executive control?’ Link back to Problem 2B.
DiagnosisCentral executive; inhibition, updating, shifting; the lexicon is organised by meaning.
TreatmentExplain why letter retrieval can’t run on automatic spreading activation, list the executive steps, then add Bozeat’s anomia caveat.
  • The lexicon is organised by meaning, not first letter: automatic spreading activation won’t deliver ‘F-words’, so retrieval must be strategic.
  • Maintain the rule for a minute (F-words, no names); plan sub-cues (fa-, fe-, fl-, fr-).
  • Monitor and update which words you’ve said (no repeats); inhibit invalid or tempting responses; shift sub-cluster when one runs dry.
  • That is the central executive (inhibition, updating, shifting); performance is sensitive to frontal-lobe function.
  • Twist: SD patients scored low, but Bozeat et al. attribute it to anomia, not executive deficit: no test is process-pure.
🪝 Memory hook: FAS = a search with the map upside-down 🗺️: you must steer by hand.
★ KEY INSIGHT · Your word store is sorted by meaning, like a library sorted by topic. Finding words by first letter means wandering the shelves with a plan, checking and skipping: that’s your brain’s manager at work.
Tap to open ▸

Letter fluency is an executive task because the lexicon is organised by meaning rather than by initial letter, so words starting with F cannot be retrieved through automatic spreading activation. Instead, the person must use controlled, strategic retrieval under the central executive: keep the rule active in working memory, generate search strategies (e.g. ‘fl-’, ‘fr-’), monitor and update which words have already been produced, inhibit rule-breaking or repeated responses, and shift to a new subcategory when one is exhausted. This covers the executive functions of inhibition, updating and shifting, and such tasks are sensitive to frontal-lobe function.

However, the task also depends on an intact vocabulary: in Bozeat et al.’s patients, poor letter fluency was attributed to anomia rather than executive dysfunction, showing that fluency scores must be interpreted alongside semantic ability.

  • Saying ‘it measures vocabulary’ without the control processes.
  • Not naming the executive functions (inhibition, updating, shifting) or the central executive.
  • Missing Bozeat et al.’s own caveat about anomia.

Exit · Waar of niet waar?
🧠 In-depth question · Exit

Exit: write (and answer) hard true/false questions

❓ Canvas question Exit, word for word
Exit
Level up je leerproces— Daag jezelf uit en bedenk als groepje in ieder geval twee moeilijke waar-niet-waar vragen.

🇬🇧 In English: Level up your learning: challenge yourself and, as a group, come up with at least two difficult true/false questions.

🩺 Triage: how to recognise and attack it
SymptomA generation task: write questions, don’t answer them.
DiagnosisEverything in the theme: the best T/F items hinge on precise distinctions.
TreatmentPick a fine distinction, change exactly one element, and keep a one-line justification ready.
  • Good items change one element of a true statement: a number, a direction, a study, a term.
  • Target confusable pairs: omission vs intrusion, prototype vs exemplar, Keil vs Rips, category vs feature verification.
  • Use exact values: 22%, 1,595 / 14 / 1, r = .96–.99, 0.59 vs 0.29.
  • Avoid trivia; aim at the logic (why a finding hurts a theory).
  • Practise on the 10 items in the 🎯 chip and check the explanations.
🪝 Memory hook: Change one thing, keep it plausible 🎭.
★ KEY INSIGHT · A hard true/false question looks almost exactly like something from the reading but has one small detail swapped, so you can only answer it if you really understand.
Tap to open ▸

Two examples of hard items: (1) ‘In Bozeat et al. (2003), animals had more omissions than artefacts.’ False: there was no domain effect on omissions; animals had more intrusions, and even that effect disappeared once feature distinctiveness was controlled. (2) ‘A strictly hierarchical network predicts no typicality effect in category verification.’ True: robin and penguin are both one link from BIRD, so only a network with variable link strengths (Collins & Loftus, 1975) predicts faster verification for typical members.

1. A sink is a clear, undisputed member of ‘kitchen utensils’.

Hampton (1979): sinks were only barely included: a borderline member.

2. Family resemblance theory says typical items share features frequent in their category AND few features of other categories.

Both parts (Rosch & Mervis, 1975).

3. Typicality is mainly caused by how often we encounter a member.

Frequency has some effect but is not the most important variable (rugs vs tables).

4. Experts often use a more specific basic level than novices.

Birdwatchers say sparrow (Tanaka & Taylor, 1991).

5. In a strictly hierarchical network, ‘a robin is a bird’ and ‘a penguin is a bird’ should take equally long.

Both are one link from BIRD; only variable link strengths predict typicality.

6. Exemplar theory can easily explain why people ‘recognise’ a never-seen prototype.

There is no stored exemplar of something never encountered (Posner et al., 1967).

7. Ad hoc categories show no typicality gradient.

Even ‘things to take on vacation’ is graded (swimsuit vs deck of cards).

8. In Bozeat et al. (2003), animals had more omissions than artefacts.

No domain effect on omissions; animals had more INTRUSIONS.

9. The animal–artefact difference in intrusions disappeared once feature distinctiveness was taken into account.

Domain effect = feature-distribution effect.

10. SD patients performed within the control range on delayed copying of geometric shapes.

Rules out an episodic explanation of poor delayed copying.

  • Writing trivia (dates, page numbers) instead of conceptual distinctions.
  • Making ‘false’ items false for two reasons at once: change only one element.

Murphy, Categories and Concepts (NOBA)

Block A · What Categories Are Like

❓ What are everyday categories really like, and what kind of mental representation can explain that?

🌫️A.1

What concepts are for, and why definitions fail

❓ This lecture answers: What is a category vs a concept, and can categories be defined by necessary and sufficient features?
A.1.1
Categories and concepts

🗂️ A category is a set of things treated as equivalent (trucks, trout); a concept is its mental representation. Concepts let you extend what you learned from a few objects to a potentially infinite set of new ones.

A.1.2
The traditional idea: categories have definitions

📏 The old view: categories are well-defined by necessary and jointly sufficient features. It fails: a dog that lost her bark is still a dog; some necessary features (blood, breathing) are not sufficient; Pluto (2006) showed "planet" had no definition.

A.1.3
Fuzzy categories: borderline members

🌫️ Hampton (1979): membership is a continuum (sinks barely utensils, sponges barely not). McCloskey & Glucksberg (1978): asked twice, two weeks apart, people changed their minds on borderline items up to 22 percent of the time. Categories are fuzzy.

INTERACTIVE · BE YOUR OWN McCLOSKEY & GLUCKSBERG

🔁 Do you agree with yourself?

Answer each question. Then press "Two weeks later…": the same questions come back in a new order with your answers hidden. See how often you change your mind.

Round 1
🌅
THINK OF IT LIKE…Day turning into night. Noon is clearly day and midnight clearly night, but at dusk people disagree, and you might answer differently on different evenings. Categories have dusk zones too.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Fuzziness just means people don't know enough about the items."
✓ CORRECTThe categories themselves are fuzzy: the same person answers differently on different days (McCloskey & Glucksberg, 1978).
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDYou'd think "dog" has a simple definition, but it doesn't: a three-legged dog that doesn't bark is still a dog. And for in-between things, like whether an olive is a fruit, people even give different answers two weeks later.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKDefinitions are neat; the world is messy.
✎ EXAM TIPWhen asked why the classical view fails, name both problems with evidence: no necessary-and-sufficient features (dog, planet) and fuzzy boundaries (Hampton, 1979; McCloskey & Glucksberg, 1978, up to 22%).
▶ Find a video: classical view and fuzzy categories
✅ Quick check: Why is McCloskey & Glucksberg stronger evidence than disagreement between people?

Disagreement between people could come from different knowledge. A person disagreeing with themselves two weeks later shows the boundary itself is unclear.

✅ Quick check: Why does "all dogs have blood and breathe" fail as a definition of dog?

Those features are necessary (every dog has them) but not sufficient: you have blood and breathe too, and you are not a dog.

🎯A.2

Typicality and family resemblance

❓ This lecture answers: Why are some members "better" examples, and what makes something typical?
A.2.1
Some members are better than others

🏆 Some members are better examples (Rosch, 1973): robins are typical birds, penguins atypical. Typicality affects nearly everything: membership judgements, speed (Rips et al., 1973), learning order (Rosch & Mervis, 1975), even word order ("apples and lemons").

A.2.2
Typicality and fuzziness: two sides of one coin

🌅 Call the most typical member the category prototype. The less similar an item is to it, the less typical, until you doubt it belongs (is a rug furniture?). Typicality fading produces borderline members.

A.2.3
What makes something typical? Family resemblance

👪 Not frequency (Rosch, Simpson & Miller, 1976) but family resemblance theory (Rosch & Mervis, 1975): a typical item has features that are frequent in the category and lacks features that are frequent in other categories.

Typicality influences…Source
Typical items are judged category members more oftenHampton (1979)
Categorisation is faster for typical itemsRips, Shoben & Smith (1973)
Typical members are learned before atypical onesRosch & Mervis (1975)
A category is learned more easily if typical examples are givenMervis & Pani (1980)
References to typical members are understood more easilyGarrod & Sanford (1977)
People mention typical items first ("apples and lemons", not "lemons and apples")Onishi, Murphy & Bock (2008)
INTERACTIVE · RATE IT YOURSELF

🍎 How typical is each fruit?

Drag each slider (1 = poor example, 7 = excellent example), then compare with Rosch & Mervis: orange and banana came first, date and tomato last.

👨‍👩‍👧‍👦
THINK OF IT LIKE…A family photo: no single feature is shared by everyone (not everyone has the nose or the curls), but the child who has most of the family's features "looks most like a family member". That is where the name family resemblance comes from.
✗ THE MISTAKE"A robin is typical because we see so many robins."
✓ CORRECTFrequency matters only a little (Rosch, Simpson & Miller, 1976). Typicality depends on family resemblance: sharing features with other members, and not with other categories. (A table and a rug are seen equally often, yet the table is far more typical.)
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDSome birds are just "birdier" than others. A robin is a great bird, a penguin a weird one, not because you see robins more, but because robins have what most birds have, and penguins have fish stuff like flippers.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKTypical = looks like the family, not like the neighbours.
✎ EXAM TIPLearn the two parts of family resemblance (frequent in own category; infrequent in other categories) and match each to one Rosch and Mervis (1975) experiment.
▶ Find a video: Rosch, typicality and family resemblance
✅ Quick check: Why is a bat a poor example of a mammal?

(a) It lacks many features frequent in mammals (walking on four legs on the ground), and (b) it has a feature frequent in another category: flying with wings, typical of birds.

✅ Quick check: How did Rosch & Mervis (1975) test both parts of family resemblance?

They made two new categories with arbitrary features. (a) Items with features common in their own category were learned sooner and later rated more typical. (b) Items sharing more features with the other category took longer to learn.

🪜A.3

Category hierarchies and the basic level

❓ This lecture answers: Every object belongs to many nested categories. Which level do we prefer, and why?
A.3.1
Categories within categories

🪜 Categories nest in hierarchies: brown bear → bear → mammal → vertebrate → animal → entity; desk chair → chair → furniture → artifact → object. Every object belongs to many categories at once. Which do we use?

A.3.2
The basic level: not too general, not too specific

🏷️ Brown (1958): we say "chair". Rosch et al. (1976): 1,595 basic level names, 14 subordinate, only once a superordinate. Basic words are frequent in text (Wisniewski & Murphy, 1989), easier to learn (Anglin, 1977) and faster to identify.

A.3.3
Why the basic level is basic, and why it moves

🧩 Basic categories are most differentiated: members alike, unlike other categories (Murphy & Brownell, 1985). Not fixed by nature: it moves up in industrialised societies (Berlin, 1992) and down for experts (Tanaka & Taylor, 1991). It depends on knowledge and interests.

TRY IT · NAME IT FAST

⚡ What is it?

Click the first name that comes to mind for each picture.

🐕
Picture 1 / 5
🐻
THINK OF IT LIKE…Goldilocks' porridge: "animal" is too cold (too vague to be useful), "northern brown bear" is too hot (too fussy to tell apart), "bear" is just right.
✗ THE MISTAKE"The basic level is fixed by nature, the same for everyone."
✓ CORRECTThe basic level depends on knowledge: it is more specific in less industrialised societies (Berlin, 1992) and for experts (Tanaka & Taylor, 1991).
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDEverything belongs to several categories: your chair is also furniture and a desk chair. But you'd just say "chair". That middle level is the sweet spot: chairs look alike and look different from other stuff. Experts zoom in further, like a birdwatcher who sees a sparrow, not a bird.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKBasic = Goldilocks: not too broad, not too narrow.
✎ EXAM TIPQuote Rosch et al.'s (1976) naming counts (1,595 basic, 14 subordinate, 1 superordinate) and give the differentiation explanation (Murphy & Brownell, 1985).
▶ Find a video: basic-level categories
✅ Quick check: Basic level for "smartphone" for a repair technician?

Probably more specific (a particular model), because expertise makes finer categories more differentiated for them (Tanaka & Taylor, 1991).

✅ Quick check: Do infants learn superordinates first?

Mandler (2004) argues they do. But then it is puzzling that older children struggle so much with superordinate words and with learning artificial superordinate categories (Horton & Markman, 1980; Mervis, 1987). Murphy: the question is not yet settled.

✅ Quick check: Why are superordinate and subordinate categories both less useful?

Superordinate members have little in common (what do most pieces of furniture share?). Subordinates are too similar to their neighbours (desk chair vs dining chair vs easy chair), so they are hard to tell apart.

⚖️A.4

How concepts are represented: prototypes and exemplars

❓ This lecture answers: Is a concept one summary of the category, or a memory of many examples?
INTERACTIVE · TWO THEORIES, ONE CLICK

🎯 Click anywhere to classify a new creature

Gold dots = remembered "glorps", blue dots = remembered "fribs" (invented categories). ★ marks each category's prototype (the average). Click a point: prototype theory picks the nearer ★; exemplar theory adds up similarity to every dot. Find a spot where they disagree (try near the lone gold dot on the right).

Click inside the box.
A.4.1
Prototype theory: a summary of the category

📋 Prototype theory: one summary representation, a list of weighted features (Smith & Medin, 1981). Typical items match many high-weight features; atypical ones fewer; borderline items (edible seaweed) resemble several categories or none.

A.4.2
Exemplar theory: a memory of examples

🗃️ Exemplar theory (Medin & Schaffer, 1978): the concept is your remembered examples; add up similarity per category, highest total wins. Allen & Brooks (1991): new items very like an old one were put in its category, even against a rule.

A.4.3
Which theory wins?

⚖️ Exemplar theory wins most lab studies, but these repeat a few examples, and we also learn from general statements, so a summary is needed too. Many accept multiple systems: descriptions, memories of particular dogs, rules (a baseball strike) (Maddox & Ashby, 2004).

📋 PROTOTYPE THEORY (Smith & Medin, 1981)
One summary: features weighted by how often they occur (wings, feathers: high; eats worms: lower; lives in Antarctica: low but not zero). Classify by matching to each summary.
Typical = many high-weight features. Borderline = resembles several summaries or none (edible seaweed).
🗃️ EXEMPLAR THEORY (Medin & Schaffer, 1978)
No summary: the concept is the stored examples. Classify by adding up similarity to all examples of each category; highest total wins.
Allen & Brooks (1991): a new item very similar to an old one is put in the old category, even against a rule.
📋 Prototype🗃️ Exemplar
StoredOne weighted summaryMany examples
Classify byMatching the item to each summaryAdding up similarity to all stored examples per category
Typicality✅ many high-weight features✅ resembles many examples
EvidenceWe learn from general statements ("Komodo dragons grow to 10 feet")Allen & Brooks (1991); wins most lab comparisons
Weak spotLoses most lab comparisonsLabs repeat few examples; real life rarely does; general statements need a summary
Many researchers now accept multiple systems: summaries, remembered examples and, for some categories, explicit rules (Maddox & Ashby, 2004).
📸
THINK OF IT LIKE…Prototype = one blended "average face" of all your friends. Exemplar = your whole photo album, flipped through every time you meet someone new.
✗ THE MISTAKEUsing "prototype" only for the most typical member.
✓ CORRECTTwo uses: the most typical member (A.2) and the theory that a concept is a summary of weighted features (A.4).
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDThere are two ideas about what's in your head when you think "bird". Either one summary, like a checklist of bird-ish features with some ticked harder than others, or all the birds you've ever seen, and you compare new things to them. Probably we use both.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKPrototype = one average; exemplar = many examples.
✎ EXAM TIPFor any finding, ask what each theory predicts. Allen and Brooks (1991) is the classic exemplar result; learning from general statements needs a summary.
▶ Find a video: prototype vs exemplar theory
✅ Quick check: A child calls a cow "dog" because it looks like the family dog. Which theory?

Exemplar theory: the cow is very similar to one strongly remembered example (the family dog), so it lands in that category.

✅ Quick check: How does prototype theory handle edible seaweed?

Borderline items may resemble several categories, or none: seaweed has few vegetable features but is not close to meat, fish or fruit either, so it matches no summary well and you feel unsure.

✅ Quick check: Why does Allen & Brooks (1991) support exemplar theory?

People had learned a rule, yet a new item that closely resembled an old one was put in the old item's category, against the rule. Similarity to a remembered example won, as an exemplar process predicts.

🦝A.5

Knowledge, essentialism and culture

❓ This lecture answers: How does world knowledge shape concepts, and why do people believe in hidden essences?
A.5.1
The knowledge approach: concepts must make sense

🏗️ Knowledge approach: we link new concepts to what we know. Murphy & Allopenna (1994): a sensible donker (under water, reached by submarine) is learned much faster than a nonsensical blegdav (desert, submarine, polar bears). Knowledge helps (tablets) and misleads.

A.5.2
Psychological essentialism

🧬 Psychological essentialism (Gelman, 2003; Medin & Ortony, 1989): belief that something hidden beneath natural kinds causes their features. Keil (1989): a raccoon made to look like a skunk is still a raccoon; a rebuilt coffeepot is a bird feeder.

A.5.3
Concepts across cultures, and the conclusion

🌏 Cultures differ somewhat (Norenzayan et al., 2002) but share many categories, so differences may be smaller than experiments suggest. Conclusion: we learn "baby" from exemplars, general descriptions, general knowledge and rules, probably in different brain structures (Maddox & Ashby, 2004).
