🏗️ Does it make sense? Think like Murphy & Allopenna

Tap an answer for each row. All examples are from your Word notes.

VOTE · WHAT IS IT NOW? (A.5.2)

🗳️ Keil-style transformations

Rows 1–2 are Keil's (1989) two conditions; row 3 is an illustrative case taken from the Word check question.

SORT IT · MURPHY'S CONCLUSION (A.5.3)

👶 Four ways you learn the concept "baby"

You visit a friend's new baby and already know what to expect. Where does each piece of knowledge come from? (Murphy's example)

🧠 These processes are probably carried out by different brain structures (Maddox & Ashby, 2004). 🌏 Across cultures: some suggest Eastern and Western modes of thought lead to qualitatively different concepts (Norenzayan, Smith, Kim & Nisbett, 2002), but cultures also share many categories (chairs, dogs, parties, jars) because the structure of the world limits which categories are useful. So the differences may be smaller than experiments designed to detect them suggest.

✗ THE MISTAKE"Essentialism is just the classical view again."
✓ CORRECTBoth give sharp boundaries, but the classical view uses visible defining features; essentialism a hidden cause that may not show at all (Keil's raccoon).
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDConcepts have to make sense: an underwater building you reach by submarine is easy to learn, a desert building with polar bears isn't. And people think animals have a hidden "essence": paint a raccoon to look like a skunk and everyone still says it's a raccoon, but rebuild a coffeepot into a bird feeder and it's a bird feeder.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKRaccoons keep their essence; coffeepots don't.
✎ EXAM TIPFor essentialism, give Keil (1989) with both conditions (raccoon versus coffeepot) and the three signs of essentialism.
▶ Find a video: essentialism and Keil's raccoon
✅ Quick check: Why can't prototype and exemplar theories alone predict Murphy & Allopenna (1994)?

They put no limits on which features you learn: every feature is just a feature. The donker is easier only because its features fit together with world knowledge, which those theories leave out.

✅ Quick check: Why is Keil's coffeepot condition important?

It shows people do not simply refuse every transformation: a rebuilt coffeepot is a bird feeder. Only the natural kind (raccoon) keeps its identity, so people treat natural kinds, not artifacts, as having an essence.

✅ Quick check: When does essentialism become harmful?

When it is applied to people. Treating gender, racial and ethnic groups as having essences exaggerates group differences and can be used to justify discrimination (Hirschfeld, 1996), as in the old belief in "bad blood".

Robinson-Riegler & Robinson-Riegler, pp. 198–207

Block B · How Knowledge Is Stored

❓ How is our knowledge of concepts organised and retrieved, and which theory of concept representation holds up best?

🕸️B.1

Semantic networks and spreading activation

❓ This lecture answers: How are concepts linked, and why does "yellow" make you recognise "lemon" faster?
INTERACTIVE · SPREADING ACTIVATION

🕸️ Click a concept and watch activation spread

Activation spreads along links, fades with distance and time, divides when many links leave a node and is summed at each node. Nodes that pass the threshold light up (Collins & Loftus, 1975). Network after Robinson-Riegler Fig. 5.11 (simplified).

Try "yellow", then "fire".
B.1.1
The question, and how to test it

⏱️ How is knowledge acquired, stored and retrieved? In a category verification task ("A robin is a bird") or feature verification task ("A cat has skin") the measure is speed: robin beats penguin, pointy ears beat skin (proximity).

B.1.2
Semantic networks

🕸️ A semantic network stores concepts as nodes joined by meaningful links ("close" = close in meaning). It is not a neural network: there is no "canary neuron". Both share excitatory connections.

B.1.3
Spreading activation and semantic priming

⚙️ Spreading activation model (Collins & Loftus, 1975): a presented node is activated; activation spreads, decreases with time and distance, gives less to each of many nodes, and is summed to a threshold. This explains semantic priming.

INTERACTIVE · SEMANTIC PRIMING

⏱️ Word or not?

A prime word flashes, then a target. Press Word or Not a word as fast as you can. After 16 trials we compare your speed for targets after a related vs an unrelated prime. illustrative word pairs.

ready?
💡
THINK OF IT LIKE…Christmas lights wired together: switch on "yellow" and the bulbs nearby (sun, lemon, canary) glow a little, so they flash on faster when it's their turn. Bulbs far away barely flicker.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Faster verification of robin is a new effect, separate from Block A."
✓ CORRECTIt is the typicality effect (Rips, Shoben & Smith, 1973), now explained as a short link in the network.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDYour knowledge is like a web of ideas. Hear "yellow", and "lemon", "sun" and "canary" light up a bit, so you'll recognise "lemon" faster a second later. And "robin is a bird" is quicker to confirm than "penguin is a bird" because robin sits closer to bird in the web.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKCloser in the web = faster to verify; activation spreads, fades and adds up.
✎ EXAM TIPKnow the four processing assumptions of Collins and Loftus (1975) and use them to explain semantic priming step by step.
▶ Find a video: spreading activation▶ Find a video: semantic priming
✅ Quick check: Why is speed, not accuracy, the measure in verification tasks?

The questions are easy and people almost never err unless they rush, so accuracy hardly varies. Speed does vary, and it reveals how closely a concept or feature is linked to the category.

✅ Quick check: Why would "doctor" speed up "nurse" but not "bread"?

Doctor and nurse are linked in the network, so activation spreads from doctor and gives nurse a head start towards its threshold. Bread is not linked to doctor, so it receives no extra activation.

🧭B.2

Concepts and categories: four approaches

❓ This lecture answers: What do concepts do, what types of category exist, and how do the classical, prototype, exemplar and essentialist approaches fare?
B.2.1
What concepts do for us

🧱 "Building blocks of thought" (Solomon, Medin & Lynch, 1999). Concepts are a mental shorthand for understanding, and support predictions (a reality show has a prize), learning and communication (Medin & Rips, 2005).

B.2.2
Types of categories

🌹 From most to least similar members (Goldstone & Kersten, 2003): natural kinds (flowers), artifacts (tools), ad hoc categories (things to take on vacation; Barsalou, 1983), metaphorical concepts (an emotional prison).

B.2.3
The classical view, and its three problems

📏 Similarity-based approaches compare an item with a stored standard. The classical view uses necessary and sufficient features (Bruner et al., 1956). Three flaws: no defining features, the typicality effect (Rosch, 1973), fuzzy boundaries.

B.2.4
The prototype approach and Posner’s dot patterns

⭐ Prototype approach: features members are likely to have; family resemblance to an abstracted prototype. Posner et al. (1967): an unseen prototype was "recognised". Problems: features that go together (Mervis & Rosch, 1981), context (Roth & Shoben, 1983), conceptual combination (Hampton, 1993).

B.2.5
The exemplar approach

🗃️ Exemplar approach: stored examples, chosen by context (Ross & Spalding, 1994). Explains typicality, context and correlations (Malt & Smith, 1984). Problems: Posner's unseen prototype; economy (Komatsu, 1992). People use both (Malt, 1989).

B.2.6
The essentialist approach: concepts as theories

🔬 The three views above are bottom-up. Essentialist approaches are top-down: a theory of the hidden essence (Medin & Ortony, 1989). Rips (1989): the excerpt ends mid-sentence, so use Keil (A.5).

INTERACTIVE · POSNER, GOLDSMITH & WELTON (1967)

🔵 Study these dot patterns

Look at the 6 patterns for 12 seconds. Then 4 patterns appear: click the one you think you saw before. In the real study every studied pattern was a distortion of a prototype that was never shown, yet people confidently "recognised" the prototype: they had been abstracting the average during study.

ApproachCompares with…SolvesProblems
📏 ClassicalNecessary & sufficient features (Bruner et al., 1956)Well-defined concepts (triangle)No defining features; typicality; fuzzy
⭐ PrototypeAbstracted average / best exampleAll 3 classical problems; Posner et al. (1967)Correlated properties (Mervis & Rosch, 1981); context (Roth & Shoben, 1983); pet fish (Hampton, 1993)
🗃️ ExemplarStored individual examplesTypicality; context; correlations (Malt & Smith, 1984)Posner's unseen prototype; economy (Komatsu, 1992)
🔬 EssentialistTheory of the hidden essenceCategorisation beyond surface similarity (Rips, 1989)Excerpt ends here; see A.5 for essentialism evidence
🐟
THINK OF IT LIKE…The typical "pet fish" is a guppy or goldfish, but neither is a prototype of "pet" or of "fish" (Hampton, 1993). Combining concepts doesn't just average two prototypes, which is a problem for prototype theory.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Blocks A and B describe different theories."
✓ CORRECTThey describe the same theories: Murphy's prototype and exemplar theories (A.4) and essentialism (A.5) are Robinson-Riegler's prototype, exemplar and essentialist approaches (B.2). Block B adds the classical view's formal problems, Posner et al. (1967) and each theory's extra problems.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDThere are four ideas about what a concept is: a strict definition, an average "best example", a pile of remembered examples, or a theory about what something really is deep down. Definitions mostly fail. Prototypes and examples each win some battles, and people probably use both.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKClassical fails; prototype averages; exemplar remembers; essence explains.
✎ EXAM TIPFor each approach, learn one supporting finding and one problem: prototype (Posner; correlated properties), exemplar (context, correlations; Posner, economy).
▶ Find a video: Posner's dot patterns▶ Find a video: ad hoc categories
✅ Quick check: Why are prototype members processed faster?

The most representative members are accessed more quickly, learned faster and more easily primed by the category name. In network terms, the distance between the category label and its prototype is short.

✅ Quick check: Why is Posner et al. (1967) a problem for the extreme exemplar approach?

People "recognised" a prototype they had never seen, so there was no stored exemplar of it to retrieve. They must have abstracted a summary during study.

✅ Quick check: Summer: "lemonade" is a typical drink; winter: "hot chocolate". Which approach explains this best?

The exemplar approach: context primes certain stored examples (just as December brings "Jingle Bells" to mind as a song). A single fixed prototype cannot shift with context (Roth & Shoben, 1983).

Bozeat et al. (2003), Cognitive Neuropsychology

Block C · When Concepts Fall Apart

❓ What does the gradual loss of concepts in semantic dementia reveal about how conceptual knowledge is structured?

🧠C.1

Semantic dementia and the structure of semantic memory

❓ This lecture answers: Why study a disease, and is semantic memory a hierarchy or a web of shared features?
C.1.1
Why study a disease to understand concepts?

🔧 Semantic dementia (temporal lobe atrophy) causes a very selective loss of semantic memory. The same items fail in every task (item consistency), independent of modality: evidence for a unitary, central system (Caramazza et al., 1990).

C.1.2
Two views of how semantic memory is structured

🪜 Hierarchical (Warrington, 1975): duck → swan → bird → animal (Hodges et al., 1995). Feature-based: categories emerge from shared features; typicality = closeness to the average (centroid) (Garrard et al., 2001). Living things have more shared features than artefacts.

C.1.3
Why use drawing as a test?

✏️ Drawing is non-verbal feature listing: it avoids anomia, is easy and gives rich data. Drawbacks: drawing skill, and "looks good" says nothing about content. Fix: features most controls draw = targets (Lambon Ralph et al., 1998).

ANIMATION · 18 MONTHS IN 4 STEPS

🦆 How one patient named a duck (Hodges, Graham & Patterson, 1995)

time 1time 2time 3time 4
"duck" 🦆
Specific knowledge is still there.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Duck → swan → bird → animal proves a stored hierarchy."
✓ CORRECTFeature networks with no built-in hierarchy produce the same pattern (Rogers et al., 2002a): distinctive features go first.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDSemantic dementia slowly wipes out what things are, while leaving speech, seeing and problem-solving mostly fine. That makes it a perfect window on how concepts are built. And drawing is a clever test: you don't need words, and you can see exactly which features of a duck someone still knows.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKShared features are sturdy; distinctive features are fragile.
✎ EXAM TIPBe able to contrast the hierarchical view (Warrington, 1975; duck → animal) with the feature-based view (Garrard et al., 2001; McRae & Cree, 2002; Rogers et al., 2002a).
▶ Find a video: semantic dementia explained
✅ Quick check: Why doubt a simple stored hierarchy?

Block A's three reasons, repeated by Bozeat et al.: some concepts are more typical than others (Rosch, 1973); membership is sometimes unclear, or an item seems to belong to several categories; and some categories are much more coherent than others (vehicles versus household items).

✅ Quick check: Why is semantic dementia especially informative?

It causes a very selective loss of conceptual knowledge while speech, visuospatial skills, problem solving and day-to-day memory stay relatively good, and the same items fail across modalities. So it shows the structure of the semantic system itself.

🦆C.2

A duck with four legs: Bozeat et al.'s two studies

❓ This lecture answers: What do patients' drawings show about which features are lost and which survive?
INTERACTIVE · DRAG THE SEVERITY

🦆 Watch a duck lose its "duckness"

Slide from healthy to severe. Distinctive features vanish first; features shared by many animals survive, and can even intrude (four legs). illustrative drawing based on the pattern Bozeat et al. describe.

healthymildmoderateseverevery severe
C.2.1
Study 1: drawing from a name

👥 6 patients drew 64 items from their names. Scoring: targets = features in ≥ 6 of 8 control drawings. Patients mean .53 vs controls .95, correlating extremely strongly with naming (r = .96–.99). Qualitative: semantically related errors; living things turned prototypical, artefacts box-like.

C.2.2
Study 2: copying, omissions and intrusions

✏️ Drawing from name needs the word, so 3 new patients also did immediate and delayed copying (~10 s). Errors rose from copy to name. Omissions: not domain-specific; intrusions: more for animals, until each feature's distinctiveness score was included.

C.2.3
What it all means

🏛️ A unitary, amodal semantic system: consistency of performance (drawing tracks verbal tasks; copying spared) and consistency of errors (patients over-extend typical names). Visual knowledge seems to interact with and depend on semantics; a separate structural description system explains this less well.

  • 📊Total errors: immediate copy < delayed copy < drawing from name, and DS < DC < IF. If a name meant nothing, a non-perceptual prompt was given (duck: "a bird that swims on ponds, waddles on land, and lays eggs").
  • ➖Omissions: no domain difference; distinctive features omitted most (F = 186.23).
  • ➕Intrusions: more for animals, domain-shared features most (F = 19.12). Animal drawings had more shared features (mean .59 per item vs .29), and once distinctiveness was included, domain no longer predicted intrusions.
  • 🔺Delayed copying of meaningless geometric shapes: all patients within the control range → the problem is semantic, not visual or episodic.
  • 🏛️Conclusion: one unitary, amodal semantic system, gradually degraded; visual knowledge partly depends on it.
🏙️
THINK OF IT LIKE…A city map fading in the rain: the little side streets (what makes a duck a duck) wash out first, while the big avenues shared by every neighbourhood (eyes, legs, "animal") stay visible, and you start drawing every animal with the same main roads.
✗ THE MISTAKE"Semantic dementia damages animal knowledge more than artefact knowledge."
✓ CORRECTOmissions didn't differ by domain, and the extra animal intrusions vanished once distinctiveness was controlled: animals just have more shared features.
💬 SAY IT TO A FRIENDPeople with semantic dementia asked to draw a duck from its name forget the special duck bits but keep the general animal bits, so they draw a duck with four legs. They can copy a picture fine, so it's not their drawing, it's their knowledge of what a duck is.
🔑 MEMORY HOOKDistinctive goes first; shared stays and spreads.
✎ EXAM TIPKnow the three conditions and their logic (immediate copy < delayed copy < from name), and the key result that domain stops predicting intrusions once distinctiveness is included.
▶ Find a video: semantic dementia drawings
✅ Quick check: Why include immediate copying?

It needs almost no semantic knowledge. Good immediate copying shows patients can see and draw; errors appearing only when memory or meaning is needed point to a semantic deficit.

✅ Quick check: Why was delayed copying of geometric shapes included?

Delayed copying of real objects draws on episodic and semantic memory. Meaningless shapes have almost no semantic content, so if patients copy them normally after a delay (they did), the failure with real objects isolates the semantic part.

✅ Quick check: Why prefer one amodal system over a separate structural description system?

A separate visual store (Riddoch et al., 1988) cannot explain why drawing correlates so strongly with verbal tasks, or why distinctive visual features are more vulnerable than shared ones. The errors also match those in naming, definition and sorting (Hodges et al., 1994, 1995).

✅ Quick check: What makes drawing a useful semantic test?

It reveals fine gradations of knowledge, because a patient can omit or add single features, whereas naming forces one label. Delayed copying assesses semantic memory with no verbal input or output, is quick and gives rich data.

🧵 Synthesis: one idea, three readings

A concept is not a definition but a structured bundle of features that differ in how widely they are shared, organised by similarity and by knowledge.

📄 Theme 4 on one page

🌫️A1

Definitions fail

Hardly any category has necessary and sufficient features; borders are fuzzy and people even change their minds (22%). Why it matters: concepts are not definitions.
🎯A2

Typicality

Some members are better (robin > penguin) because they share many features with their category and few with others: family resemblance. Why it matters: typicality shapes speed, learning and language.
🪜A3

Basic level

We prefer the middle level ("chair"): members alike, other categories different. It shifts with culture and expertise. Why it matters: it is where concepts are most useful.
⚖️A4

Prototype vs exemplar

Store one weighted summary, or many remembered examples? Both explain typicality; real concepts probably use both, plus rules. Why it matters: this is the core theory debate.
🦝A5

Knowledge & essence

Sensible concepts are learned faster (donker); natural kinds feel like they have a hidden essence (Keil's raccoon). Why it matters: concepts depend on what we know.
🕸️B1

Semantic networks

Concepts as linked nodes; activation spreads, fades and sums, which explains faster verification of typical items and priming. Why it matters: a model of how knowledge is retrieved.
🧭B2

Four approaches

Classical fails (no definitions, typicality, fuzzy edges); prototype (Posner) and exemplar (context, correlations) each win some, lose some; essence adds a top-down view. Why it matters: no single theory is complete.
🧠C1

Semantic dementia

Selective loss of concepts; the question is whether knowledge is stored in a hierarchy or as shared and distinctive features. Why it matters: breakdown reveals structure.
🦆C2

A duck with four legs

Errors rise with reliance on concepts and with severity; distinctive features are lost first, shared ones intrude, so drawings turn prototypical; the domain effect is really a feature effect. Why it matters: one central, feature-based semantic system.
💬 The whole theme to a friend: "Your idea of 'bird' isn't a dictionary definition. It's a bundle of features, some shared by almost all birds, some special to one kind, and the robin is the best bird because it has the most common ones. When people with semantic dementia lose concepts, the special features go first and the common ones stay and spill over. That's why they draw a duck with four legs."

Sources: Murphy (NOBA), Categories and Concepts · Robinson-Riegler & Robinson-Riegler, pp. 198–207 · Bozeat et al. (2003), Cognitive Neuropsychology. Video buttons open a YouTube search so you can pick a current video.
